lessons.title: From assessed risk to an engineered security lifecycle
lessons.body:
IC34 begins where an assessment becomes an implementable engineering obligation. The input is not just a list of vulnerabilities. It is a defined system, credible scenarios, consequence and operating constraints, zone/conduit hypotheses, required security properties, unresolved assumptions and accountable risk decisions. Read the IC33 risk and requirements artifacts first. A design that solves a scanner finding while breaking the process or leaving the actual trust path open has not met the engineering objective.

Organize the work into linked baselines. The requirements baseline states what the system must do, reject, preserve and recover under defined conditions. The conceptual architecture assigns functions and trust boundaries without prematurely fixing every implementation detail. Detailed design specifies devices, interfaces, identity flows, rules, software baselines, monitoring, failure handling and recovery. The implemented baseline records what was actually installed. Verification checks whether that implementation meets specified requirements; validation asks whether the resulting system is suitable for the intended operational use. Both require evidence and both can reveal a need to revise an earlier assumption.

Use a traceable lifecycle rather than a one-pass checklist. An assessment finding may require a mediated vendor path. Concept design places an access intermediary and separates maintenance from process control. Detailed design specifies authentication, target restrictions, session revocation, logging and emergency access. Implementation produces configurations and procedures. Factory testing exercises the representative mechanisms; site testing verifies actual routes, identities, physical interfaces and operating dependencies. Handover assigns maintenance and monitoring. A later supplier or load change can reopen the assessment. The sequence is iterative, but changes must remain controlled and visible.

Assign responsibility for each decision and artifact. The asset owner defines acceptable process behavior and owns eligible residual-risk acceptance. Designers and integrators propose and implement controls within the agreed scope. Operations and maintenance verify that the workflow is usable and sustainable. Safety specialists qualify safety-related assumptions through their own discipline. Suppliers provide supported configurations, compatibility information and component evidence. The same person may fill several roles, but the review should distinguish technical authorship, independent verification and authority to accept consequences.

Make review gates evidence-based. A concept review asks whether all relevant paths and dependencies are represented and whether the architecture can meet the requirements. A detailed-design review asks whether configurations, interfaces and failure behavior are specific enough to implement and test. A factory readiness review checks the representative baseline, test procedures, expected outcomes and restoration arrangements. A site readiness review checks installed differences, approved change windows, operational monitoring and rollback. Acceptance requires resolved or explicitly owned deviations, not merely completion of the installation schedule.

Configuration control is essential because evidence is baseline-specific. Record product and firmware versions, configuration identifiers, application packages, certificate/trust material references, project files and dependency versions without exposing secrets. A test on gateway firmware 5.1 does not automatically validate a site running 5.2 with different session behavior. Assess the difference, identify affected requirements and repeat the relevant tests. This is more precise than either accepting every newer version without review or repeating every test for an irrelevant documentation edit.

Security engineering must include degraded and recovery states. A remote-access system that works only while the primary directory is healthy may obstruct the recovery it is intended to support. A log collector that fails silently can invalidate detection requirements. A failover path may restore connectivity while bypassing the application restriction. Specify the intended behavior under component loss and verify that the system returns to a trusted normal state. This original programme uses synthetic cases and offline models; real commissioning requires supported platforms, authorized changes and qualified process oversight. Completing it supports preparation but does not replace ISA's required course and examination.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — DESIGN PROJECT BASELINE (synthetic): Risk K1 is unauthorized vendor setpoint change through a cellular bypass. Requirement R1: every vendor engineering session shall traverse owner-controlled intermediary M; direct paths shall be disabled. R2: active-session revocation within 60 seconds. R3: local control shall continue during M failure; approved emergency engineering shall be available within 30 minutes without directory D. Factory baseline uses M firmware 5.1 and an independent emergency account. Site plan uses 5.2, keeps the cellular modem for commissioning, and stores emergency-account approval in an application requiring D. Factory tests show allowed session success and new-login denial after account disablement; they do not test active-session revocation or M/D loss. The installer proposes acceptance after all equipment powers on.
worked_examples.solution:
Power-on verifies only a narrow installation condition. It does not show that K1 is treated or that R1–R3 hold. The retained cellular modem contradicts complete mediation until it is disabled or brought under a specifically approved temporary arrangement with closure before the relevant acceptance gate. The new-login test does not verify R2 because an already issued session may retain authority. R3 has two separate obligations: local control continuity and emergency engineering without D. The site approval application creates a circular dependency that the independent factory account alone does not resolve.

The firmware change from 5.1 to 5.2 requires impact analysis against the relevant session, identity and failure behavior. Obtain supplier change information and inspect the actual configuration; repeat the affected tests rather than assuming equivalence. The design review should produce a trace from each requirement to mechanism, test and result, identify deviations and owners, and establish readiness for authorized site verification. The owner may decide how to handle eligible residual risks, but that decision must not be mislabeled as proof that an unmet requirement has passed.

guided_practice.prompt: Create a five-row lifecycle trace for R2, from the risk through operation. Include one evidence item at each stage.
guided_practice.hint: The same revocation behavior must remain identifiable across design, implementation, testing and maintenance.
guided_practice.solution: Risk: a revoked vendor retains process authority, supported by the session-lifetime assessment. Requirement: existing sessions lose privileged authority within sixty seconds of an authorized trigger. Detailed design: specify supported identity-to-session revocation integration and audit events. Verification: measure a previously active session attempting the relevant operation before and after revocation under representative and site conditions. Operation: assign ownership and periodically or event-triggered verify the integration after identity/gateway changes, preserving results and exception decisions.

independent_task.brief: Build a lifecycle evidence plan for R1–R3 with concept, detailed design, factory, site and handover gates.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Every requirement has an implementing mechanism and a test covering its actual conditions.
Factory/site differences and temporary access are explicit controlled deviations.
Verification evidence and owner risk acceptance remain separate decisions.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Translating the CRS into implementable controls and tests
lessons.body:
A requirements specification becomes implementable when each obligation is assigned to a mechanism capable of making the required decision. A router can select a path; a stateful firewall can track permitted sessions; an application gateway can interpret supported operations; an identity service can authenticate a principal; a controller can enforce supported role or command constraints. Assigning an application-semantic requirement to a port-only filter leaves a gap even if the filter is configured exactly as designed.

Decompose an access decision into conditions. A maintenance write may require a named identity, an approved role, an approved target, a permitted function, an active maintenance window and a fresh command. The effective authorization is the conjunction of all required conditions, not any one of them. Identify where each condition is evaluated and how the result is bound to the same session and command. If a gateway authenticates Alice but forwards commands under a shared downstream account, the design needs a reliable way to preserve the relevant attribution and prevent a different session from borrowing that authority.

Use an authorization matrix with explicit defaults. Rows can represent actor roles and columns target functions, with additional conditions recorded separately. For example, a historian may read registers but not change alarm thresholds; an engineer may change thresholds only during an approved session; a recovery role may restore an approved project under emergency authorization. State whether unlisted combinations are denied. Avoid a broad inherited role that silently overrides the intended restrictions. Review effective permissions after nesting, local overrides and service accounts are considered.

Translate timing requirements into a measurement plan. Define the trigger event, completion event, clock sources, permitted uncertainty and boundary convention. 'Revoke within sixty seconds' should identify whether completion means a token is marked invalid, the network connection closes, or the previously active session can no longer perform the protected operation. These can occur at different times. Test the protected capability directly. If two clocks can differ by plus or minus two seconds, an observed 59-second interval does not prove a 60-second bound without accounting for uncertainty or using a common trustworthy clock.

Design freshness at the layer that understands the command. A message may arrive on a new TCP connection yet contain an old application command. A queue can retain bytes through an outage and deliver them later. The receiver or trusted intermediary needs a supported way to evaluate age, sequence and relevant process state. Specify what happens at exactly the age limit, how clocks or sequence counters are trusted, how replay is handled and how rejected commands are logged. Do not reset an old command's timestamp merely because a relay forwards it.

Create acceptance cases from the requirement conditions. A positive case proves a fully authorized operation works. Negative cases vary one condition at a time to show that each is actually enforced: wrong role, wrong target, closed window, disallowed function or stale command. Combined cases test interactions, such as a revoked session that reconnects during a still-open window. Degraded cases test loss of identity, time, logging or an enforcement component according to the specified behavior. Keep tests safe by using simulated operations or a supported representative platform with process outputs isolated and approved procedures.

Maintain traceability to evidence and design decisions. For each requirement, record the enforcement point, configuration object, prerequisite services, test case, expected output and evidence artifact. Where a platform cannot meet the requirement, do not hide the limitation with a successful unrelated test. Revise the architecture, select another supported control, or obtain an explicit risk decision and requirement change through the owner. The design must still preserve necessary operations and recovery, so test rejection and service continuity together. This decomposition is the basis for the firewall, remote-access, hardening, monitoring and acceptance modules that follow.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — DESIGN CONTRACT (synthetic): H role may read G registers with function 3 only. E role may write alarm threshold register 110 with function 6, only to G, during an approved window and with command age ≤5 seconds; other writes are denied. R2 completion means a previously active session can no longer execute the protected operation within 60 seconds of revocation request. Test timestamps from a common validated clock: request at 14:00:00; identity marked disabled at 14:00:10; TCP connection remains open; last successful protected operation at 14:01:05; first confirmed denial at 14:01:08. A second test uses two clocks with independent error bounds ±2 seconds and observes denial 59 seconds after request. Gateway policy enforces identity, target and window but filters only TCP/502; it has no function/register parser. Queue Q rewrites enqueue time whenever forwarding an old command. No behavior is specified for loss of trusted time.
worked_examples.solution:
The first revocation test fails the defined sixty-second capability bound: an operation still succeeds at 65 seconds. The identity-disable flag at ten seconds and the still-open TCP connection do not determine the answer, because the requirement defines completion in terms of protected operation authority. The first denial at 68 seconds bounds one observed failed attempt, but does not repair the earlier demonstrated violation. In the second test, independent ±2-second errors can make the actual interval as much as 63 seconds; an observed 59 seconds is inconclusive for a strict sixty-second bound.

The port-only gateway cannot implement H's function-3-only role or E's register/function restriction. Add a supported semantic enforcement mechanism or endpoint authorization that can express the requirement, then test both permitted and nearby forbidden operations. Q's timestamp rewriting defeats end-to-end age evaluation and must be replaced with a trustworthy original-age or supported sequence/state mechanism. The loss-of-time behavior is an unresolved requirement: the owner must define an operationally acceptable rejection, bounded holdover or other justified mode before the design can be accepted.

guided_practice.prompt: Create six negative tests for E that each change exactly one required condition, then one combined revocation/reconnect test.
guided_practice.hint: Keep all other conditions valid so a denial can be attributed to the condition under test.
guided_practice.solution: Test a wrong role, wrong target, function 16 instead of 6, a register other than 110, a closed maintenance window and command age above five seconds. For the combined case, revoke an active E session while the window remains open, attempt the protected operation after the sixty-second bound, reconnect using retained session material, and verify the supported design rejects both old and renewed authority without a new valid authorization.

independent_task.brief: Produce a requirement-to-enforcement matrix and a timed acceptance procedure for the supplied contract.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Application semantics are assigned to a mechanism that can inspect or authorize them.
Timing results use the specified completion event and clock uncertainty.

independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Conceptual architecture and enforceable trust boundaries
lessons.body:
A conceptual architecture must show how the required trust boundaries can be enforced by the system's real paths. Start with the zone and conduit requirements from IC33, then place the process, supervisory, maintenance, shared-service and enterprise-facing functions. Draw both data and management paths. Identify where an untrusted or lower-trust principal becomes authorized to perform a higher-consequence action, and assign an enforcement mechanism to that transition. A diagram that puts a firewall icon between two colored boxes is incomplete until the forwarding path actually crosses that device.

Layer 2 and Layer 3 behavior determine whether a routed firewall can see the traffic. Hosts in the same IP subnet normally resolve each other's link-layer address and exchange frames through the local switching domain; their default gateway is not used for that local destination. Placing a firewall as their default gateway therefore does not filter their same-subnet exchanges. Separate broadcast domains, host isolation or a suitably designed transparent enforcement mechanism is needed if those exchanges must cross a boundary. The design must state which mechanism is used and how it is verified.

Different VLANs do not guarantee firewall traversal either. A multilayer switch with interfaces in both VLANs can route directly between them unless its routing/policy design sends the relevant traffic through the intended control. VRFs or other routing separation can help prevent an unintended local route, but their route imports, shared services and management paths require deliberate design. A missing return route can break an allowed session; an alternate return path can bypass monitoring or conflict with stateful inspection. Trace both directions for normal and failover states.

Use intermediaries according to their function. An enterprise-facing report proxy should expose only the required published data service, not provide arbitrary routing to controllers. A maintenance jump host should have controlled target reach and privileges rather than unrestricted membership in the process zone. A dual-homed host can bridge trust domains through IP forwarding, an application proxy, remote-control software or shared credentials even when one particular forwarding switch is disabled. Assess the host's effective capabilities and design ownership, not just its interface count.

Separate management authority from normal process data. A hypervisor administrator can alter VM disks and network attachments; a network administrator can change segmentation; an identity administrator can grant roles; a backup administrator may replace recovery images. These authorities can cross several data-plane zones. Put them in an explicit management design with justified reach, strong identities, role separation where feasible, controlled changes and evidence. An out-of-band cable improves independence only if its endpoints, access and shared dependencies are appropriately controlled.

Preserve process and safety boundaries. A local protective function may need to continue when supervisory networks fail, while its configuration access still requires cyber protection. Do not route an emergency protective action through a general-purpose intermediary merely because that simplifies centralized logging. Conversely, do not assume a protective relay is outside cyber scope if its settings can be changed through an engineering port. Work with the qualified process/safety owners to retain required independence and validate failure behavior. Security and safety architectures must be reconciled without treating their assurance labels as interchangeable.

Compare candidate architectures using path proofs and failure scenarios. For each required flow, identify source, destination, next hop, enforcement point, identity context and return path. For each forbidden flow, identify the control that blocks it and an independent test that would reveal a bypass. Then remove an intermediary, fail a link, activate the standby route and exercise the emergency workflow in the model. The chosen concept should make the intended invariant simple to explain and maintain: for example, every vendor process-changing action traverses a named authorization point. Detailed configuration and acceptance tests must later demonstrate that invariant on the installed baseline.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — CANDIDATE ARCHITECTURES (synthetic): A places historian H=10.20.0.10/24, jump host J=10.20.0.20/24 and controller C=10.20.0.30/24 in VLAN 20; firewall F=10.20.0.1 is their default gateway. A claims F filters H/J-to-C traffic. B places H in VLAN 20/subnet 10.20.0.0/24 and C in VLAN 30/subnet 10.30.0.0/24. Switch S has active routed interfaces for both VLANs in the same routing table; F is only S's default route. Candidate C removes direct inter-VLAN routing and makes F the required routed boundary with verified return paths. However, J in C has a second NIC in the controller VLAN and an application proxy to C. Hypervisor manager V can reattach all VM NICs and is reachable from enterprise administrator endpoints. C's local protective logic does not require H or F; its configuration interface does.
worked_examples.solution:
A's same-subnet H/J-to-C traffic normally uses direct Layer 2 delivery and does not traverse the default gateway F. B fixes the shared subnet but S still has connected routes to both networks, so its more-specific connected route handles inter-VLAN traffic before the default route to F. Neither candidate supports the claimed firewall mediation as described.

Candidate C can make F the routed boundary for the intended path, but J's second NIC and application proxy create another transition to the controller zone. Disabling IP forwarding alone would not remove an application proxy that originates its own downstream connection. V is also a cross-zone management authority capable of changing virtual attachments; its enterprise reach and privileges need an explicit management boundary. Preserve the controller's required local protective independence while restricting configuration access. The architecture should be accepted only after every relevant data, maintenance and management path is represented and assigned to a verifiable control.

guided_practice.prompt: For each candidate, trace H-to-C request and response without assuming a firewall icon is on-path. Then propose one correction for the actual bypass.
guided_practice.hint: Use destination subnet membership and the most specific available route before considering a default route.
guided_practice.solution: A needs an appropriate separation/enforcement mechanism because H and C communicate locally in one subnet. B needs removal or controlled separation of S’s direct inter-VLAN route, or another validated enforcement design, because connected routes win over its default. C needs J’s alternate NIC/proxy path removed or explicitly controlled under the same authorization requirements, with management V also constrained. Verify both directions and failure states after the changes.

lessons.title: Switching and routing controls at the OT boundary
lessons.body:
The switching design determines which endpoints share a broadcast domain and which links carry each zone. The routing design determines where traffic leaves that domain. Define both before writing firewall rules. For a simple architecture with a firewall as the only inter-zone router, process and supervisory ports belong to separate VLANs; the switch transports those VLANs to the firewall but does not provide an alternate routed interface between them. Management has its own justified path and authorization. This is one reference architecture, not a universal prescription for every OT installation.

Use explicit port roles. An endpoint expected to send untagged frames should be an access port in its assigned VLAN. A link carrying several approved VLANs is a trunk with a deliberately bounded allowed set. A dynamic negotiation mode can create a trunk when the peer's behavior changes; a fixed endpoint role avoids that ambiguity. The native VLAN treatment must agree at both ends of a trunk, and the firewall's tagged subinterfaces must match the intended VLAN IDs. Adding a VLAN to a diagram does not create it on the switch or permit it across a trunk.

The following fragment is an unexecuted teaching example for a Cisco Catalyst 9300 running IOS XE 17.9.x, using interfaces selected only for this synthetic lab. It is not a full production configuration or a recommendation to change a live switch. Cisco's release-specific trunk guide documents static access/trunk roles, allowed VLAN sets and disabling DTP negotiation on suitable static ports. Confirm the exact hardware, software, existing configuration and supported change procedure in any real lab.

```text
vlan 120
 name SUPERVISORY
vlan 130
 name PROCESS
vlan 900
 name MANAGEMENT
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 120
 switchport nonegotiate
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/20
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 130
 switchport nonegotiate
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/48
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 120,130,900
 switchport nonegotiate
```

This fragment separates H and C at Layer 2 and carries the three listed VLANs toward F. It does not remove an existing switch virtual interface, disable an alternate route, configure F, protect switch management or prove that the physical cable connects to the intended peer. Those are separate design and verification tasks. Review current configuration before applying a candidate change; partial configuration snippets can leave old behavior active. A management SVI can be legitimate while process SVIs create an unintended route, depending on the overall architecture.

Verify the implemented state with complementary evidence. In the stated platform family, illustrative read-only commands include `show interfaces switchport`, `show interfaces trunk`, `show vlan brief`, `show ip route`, `show ipv6 route` and `show mac address-table`. These commands are not executed here. Interpret what each reveals: configured/operational port mode, allowed and forwarding VLANs, membership, routed destinations and observed attachment. A VLAN allowed on a trunk may still fail to forward because it is absent, suspended, blocked by spanning tree or missing at the peer. A successful ping can confirm one reachability case but cannot prove all forbidden routes are absent.

Protect availability without creating hidden bypasses. Spanning tree, link aggregation and redundant trunks can change forwarding during failure; verify the allowed VLANs and enforcement path in every supported state. Endpoint-port protections must match the attached device: a port intended for one endpoint should not silently become an unmanaged switch attachment, but controls that disable a legitimate downstream bridge can also interrupt service. Validate the expected MAC count, replacement workflow and failure response in the supported environment rather than applying a generic hardening command indiscriminately.

Treat IPv6 and management as explicit scope. IPv4 segmentation does not constrain an active IPv6 route unless the design covers it. Switch administration should be restricted to the approved management path, identity and protocol; an access restriction on the switch's login service does not filter transit process traffic. Preserve an authorized recovery method before changing management reach. Finally, compare the as-built VLAN/route/interface state with the conduit requirements and test both permitted and prohibited flows under normal and failover conditions. Only that combined evidence supports the claim that the firewall is the actual inter-zone boundary.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC SWITCH REVIEW, Catalyst 9300 IOS XE 17.9.x-style data; no commands executed. H is on Gi1/0/10 and should be VLAN120. C is on Gi1/0/20 and should be VLAN130. F is connected to Gi1/0/48 with tagged subinterfaces 120,130,900. Actual switch state: Gi1/0/10 operational mode trunk, allowed VLANs all; Gi1/0/20 access VLAN130; Gi1/0/48 trunk allowed 120,900 (130 omitted). VLAN120 and130 both have active SVIs with IP routing enabled, yielding connected routes on S. Management is VLAN900. A second standby uplink U also carries all VLANs and leads to another router with both process/supervisory routes. IPv6 is enabled on H/C but no IPv6 path review exists. F counters for H-to-C remain zero during a successful application connection.
worked_examples.solution:
The intended reference fragment and actual state differ at multiple layers. H's port is an operational trunk, giving it a broader Layer 2 attachment than the assigned supervisory access role. The F trunk omits VLAN130, so the intended controller-zone link to F is incomplete. Despite that omission, the application can succeed because S's active SVIs route directly between VLAN120 and130. Zero F counters are consistent with that bypass rather than proof that the firewall correctly allowed the session.

The standby uplink is another possible bypass during normal or failure conditions; its broad allowed set and downstream router must be reconciled with the required path. Correcting only the primary trunk list does not remove S's local route or U's alternate route. Review IPv6 independently and preserve the management recovery path while implementing the approved architecture. Acceptance should verify port roles, VLAN carriage, route selection, firewall traversal and negative path tests in both primary and standby states, not merely observe one successful application connection.

guided_practice.prompt: Write an ordered verification plan that distinguishes a missing VLAN on F’s trunk from S’s direct-routing bypass.
guided_practice.hint: Check configured transport first, then trace the successful flow’s actual next hop and enforcement point.
guided_practice.solution: Confirm endpoint VLAN membership and F subinterface IDs; inspect Gi1/0/48 allowed/active/forwarding VLANs to identify missing130; inspect S’s connected routes and H/C gateway settings; reconcile MAC/ARP and route evidence with an authorized flow observation; verify whether F counters or logs see that flow. After the approved correction, confirm required service through F and denial of the former direct/standby bypass, including IPv6 and failure-state tests.

A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Endpoint access roles and trunk allowed sets match the assigned zones.
No unreviewed SVI, standby route or address family bypasses the intended boundary.
Management access and recovery remain available only through approved paths.

lessons.title: Stateful firewall configuration and revocation behavior
lessons.body:
A stateful firewall makes decisions using packet fields and connection state. The initial packet of a permitted connection creates or uses tracking information; later packets can be recognized as part of that connection. This reduces the need for broad reverse-direction permits, but it also creates a lifecycle question: removing the rule that admitted new connections may leave existing connections authorized by an earlier established-state rule. Define whether a policy change must stop only new sessions or also revoke existing authority, then design and test the required behavior.

The Linux nftables example below is a synthetic routed boundary using the `inet` family, which can handle IPv4 and IPv6. It uses long-established syntax for a representative Linux 6.1+/nftables 1.0+ lab; the exact distribution package, kernel support and complete existing ruleset must be checked in a real authorized environment. No nft command is executed in this course. The fragment covers forwarding only. It does not configure interfaces, routes, kernel forwarding, local management input/output, application-function inspection, availability or production recovery.

```text
table inet ot_boundary {
  chain forward {
    type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
    ct state invalid drop
    ct state established,related counter accept
    iifname "sup" oifname "proc" ip saddr 10.120.0.10 ip daddr 10.130.0.40 tcp dport 502 ct state new counter accept
    iifname "maint" oifname "proc" ip saddr 10.140.0.20 ip daddr 10.130.0.40 tcp dport 443 ct state new counter accept
    limit rate 5/second burst 10 packets log prefix "OT-DROP "
    counter drop
  }
}
```

The first permitted new flow is H to G on TCP/502 through the specified interfaces. The second is J to G on TCP/443. Return packets belonging to admitted tracked connections can match the established/related rule. A new G-initiated connection to H has no matching new-session permit and reaches denial. The policy does not make Modbus read-only: that requires a suitable operation-level control taught next. Its IPv4-address conditions do not allow arbitrary new IPv6 sessions; the final policy denies unmatched traffic, but existing state and other active base chains still require review in the complete system.

The log-rate rule and unconditional final drop are separate deliberately. Logging is bounded to protect resources, while every unmatched packet still reaches the drop regardless of whether it was logged. A rate-limited rule that both logs and drops can leave excess packets to subsequent rules; the final chain policy may still drop them, but the designer must understand that path. Counters describe the rules they are attached to, not necessarily every packet at the site or every application operation. Log absence can mean rate limiting, an earlier match, a different path or collection failure.

Revocation requires explicit treatment of connection and application state. In an isolated model, placing a deny for a revoked source/destination before the established-state accept can block the existing flow in the required direction. Alternatively, a supported procedure can remove relevant connection state and prevent readmission, but state deletion can affect active operations and must be coordinated. Neither approach automatically revokes a separately issued application token or an alternate path. Define the full authority chain and verify the protected operation rather than assuming a transport teardown is complete identity revocation.

Commission in controlled stages. Preserve the current baseline and an authorized recovery path, inspect the candidate for syntax and semantic scope, and apply changes through the platform's supported transaction mechanism. An illustrative `nft --check --file candidate.nft` checks command validity without applying the candidate, but does not prove policy correctness, interface routing or operational compatibility. An illustrative `nft -a list table inet ot_boundary` exposes installed objects and handles for review. Both remain unexecuted here. Use isolated representative endpoints or the supplied offline model for learning, then require owner-approved site procedures for real deployment.

Acceptance must exercise allowed new sessions, return traffic, forbidden initiation, existing-session behavior after policy change, malformed/invalid-state handling, IPv6 scope, logging under load and restoration of the approved policy. Verify actual routes so packets cross the intended hook; traffic addressed to the firewall itself uses the input path rather than this forwarding chain. Inspect the complete ruleset because another base chain or management agent can affect the final verdict. Save and verify the intended persistent configuration separately from runtime success. A firewall is commissioned when its required behavior and recovery are demonstrated on the controlled baseline, not merely when a ruleset parses.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC FIREWALL TEST LOG: Reference forwarding rules are those shown in the lesson. H=10.120.0.10, G=10.130.0.40, J=10.140.0.20. At 14:00 H opens TCP source port 41000 to G:502; request and reply pass. At 14:01 the H new-session permit is removed, but the established/related rule remains first. The existing H session still passes; a new H session using source port41001 is denied. A proposed emergency deny for H is appended after established/related. A new G→H TCP/502 session is denied. During a burst, 100 unmatched packets reach the logging section in one second; only a limited subset is logged, while the final drop counter rises by100. SSH addressed to F itself is outside this forward chain. No other base chains are included in this isolated model; real deployment must inspect them.
worked_examples.solution:
The old H session continues because the established-state rule accepts it before any later new-session restriction. Removing the admission rule successfully blocks the new source-port41001 connection, but does not meet a requirement to revoke the existing session. Appending the emergency deny after the established accept has the same ordering problem. A supported revocation design must place the relevant block before that accept or deliberately manage connection state and readmission, while also addressing application authority and operational effects.

The G-initiated denial is consistent with a narrow directional admission policy: permitted replies are not permission for arbitrary reverse initiation. The burst result is also consistent with the rule structure; bounded logging does not change the unconditional final drop count. SSH to F must be handled by a separately designed local input policy. The results demonstrate the isolated model's semantics only; they do not show that interfaces, real kernel state, persistence, other chains or process compatibility have been validated on a deployed firewall.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a safe revocation test that distinguishes old and new H sessions and proves the intended protected-operation outcome.
guided_practice.hint: Preserve connection identity and test rule ordering rather than treating all traffic from H as one observation.
guided_practice.solution: In an isolated representative setup, establish and identify one H–G session, verify an allowed harmless operation, apply the approved revocation mechanism, then attempt the same operation on the existing session and a new connection. Record timestamps, matching rule/state and application results. Verify unrelated required sessions remain functional and the approved rollback restores only the intended baseline. Do not issue live process writes or delete broad connection state without the required authorization.

independent_task.brief: Analyze the reference policy and supply a candidate revision, test matrix and rollback plan for immediate H revocation while preserving J access.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Established-state ordering is addressed and both existing/new sessions are tested.
Local firewall management and transit forwarding are not confused.
Rate-limited logs are interpreted separately from complete denial counters and actual path coverage.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Industrial protocol authorization and command integrity
lessons.body:
Industrial protocols often carry operations with very different consequences over one transport service. A TCP/502 permit can carry reads, single-register writes, multiple-register writes and other supported Modbus operations. A security requirement such as 'historian read-only' therefore needs an enforcement mechanism that understands the relevant operation or an endpoint role that denies writes. Port filtering remains useful for reducing paths, but it cannot supply application semantics that it does not inspect.

Define the authorized operation as a structured object. Include the authenticated source/session, destination device and downstream unit, function, address range, value representation, operating condition, age or sequence and required response. For a gateway serving several serial controllers, the IP address identifies the gateway while a unit identifier may select a downstream device. Permitting the correct gateway with an unrestricted unit selector can reach the wrong process asset. Record the mapping and validate it after replacement or serial readdressing.

A parser must reconstruct the application message correctly before deciding. TCP is a byte stream: one application request can span several packets, and one packet can contain more than one request. Inspecting only the first packet or assuming one request per packet can miss later operations or reject legitimate segmentation. Validate declared lengths, function-specific fields and supported encodings, and define behavior for malformed, unsupported or ambiguous messages. The enforcement platform must actually support these semantics; a custom illustrative parser is not a production industrial firewall merely because it can decode a sample.

Values require device-specific interpretation. A raw register can be signed or unsigned, scaled, bit-packed or part of a multi-register value. A number that looks small in one representation can be large or negative in another. Apply bounds to the intended engineering quantity using the approved register map, and preserve the exact raw value for evidence. A generic numerical range is not a safety guarantee: qualified process engineering determines acceptable limits, dynamics, modes and protective behavior. Cyber command validation should enforce the approved specification without claiming to replace independent protective functions.

Be careful with multi-field and multi-register operations. A function-16 write can span an allowed address and an adjacent forbidden address. Checking only the starting register is insufficient; validate the full range, count and every relevant value or reject unsupported composite operations. Some protocols support mask writes or combined read/write functions that can modify state through a different function number. An allowlist should enumerate the supported permitted operations and deny other write-capable alternatives rather than assume all writes use the one function seen during normal polling.

Bind authorization to the command's original context. The maintenance window, role and target should be checked at the required stage, including execution if a queue can delay delivery. Freshness and replay protection require supported trusted time, sequence or transaction-state mechanisms; a transaction identifier used for matching responses is not automatically a secure anti-replay token. Reconnecting a TCP session must not renew a revoked identity's authority without the required authentication and approval. Preserve relevant identity-to-command evidence even when the downstream legacy device uses a shared account or no individual authentication.

Design failure handling explicitly. An unsupported function can be rejected with an appropriate protocol response or the connection closed according to supported behavior and operational requirements. Avoid a silent parser bypass that permits traffic when inspection fails. On the other hand, malformed traffic handling must not exhaust the gateway or cause uncontrolled retries that harm availability. Test fragmented/coalesced messages, boundary values, wrong units, overlapping register ranges, revoked sessions and recovery after denial in an isolated supported environment. The resulting evidence should show both allowed operations and the nearby forbidden operations that a port-only rule would miss.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC APPLICATION POLICY: Gateway G maps unit1 to cooling controller A and unit2 to B. H may use function3 to read offsets100–101 on unit1 only. E may use function6 to write offset110 on unit1, with raw unsigned16 value180–350 inclusive representing 18.0–35.0°C, during an approved window, command age≤5 seconds and valid session. All other operations denied. Candidate inspector checks gateway IP, function in {3,6,16}, starting offset≤110, and only the first request in each TCP packet. It ignores unit ID and function16 count. Test records: T1 H/function3/unit1/start100/count2; T2 E/function6/unit2/offset110/value300; T3 E/function16/unit1/start110/count2/values300,999; T4 E/function6/unit1/offset110/value65535; T5 one TCP packet contains an allowed H read followed by an H function6 write; T6 one allowed E request is split across two TCP segments. All times/sessions are otherwise valid unless stated.
worked_examples.solution:
T1 is the intended H read: its full range is offsets100–101 on unit1. T2 targets the wrong downstream controller despite the correct gateway, function, offset and numerical value. T3 uses an unapproved function and spans offset111, so checking only its starting address fails twice. T4's unsigned raw65535 represents6553.5°C under the supplied map and exceeds the allowed range; interpreting it as signed−1 would use the wrong representation and still would not make it a valid18–35°C value.

T5 demonstrates why packet-level first-request inspection is inadequate: an allowed first message can conceal a subsequent forbidden operation in the same stream data. T6 demonstrates the opposite framing condition: a legitimate request can span packets and should be evaluated after correct reconstruction within resource limits. The candidate inspector cannot claim to implement the policy. Replace it with a supported capable enforcement design or revise the architecture, and validate each field/condition and parser behavior. The allowed range is a synthetic engineering specification, not a universal safe cooling setting or a certified protective function.

guided_practice.prompt: Add a mask-write function and a stale otherwise-valid command to the negative test plan. Explain the required decision without assuming the inspector supports them.
guided_practice.hint: The policy explicitly enumerates permitted functions and includes an age condition.
guided_practice.solution: The mask-write function is denied because it is not one of the role-specific permitted operations, even if it targets110. An E function6 write with age greater than five seconds is denied despite a valid role, unit, offset and value. If the platform cannot recognize these conditions reliably, record a design capability gap and select a supported mechanism rather than claiming the port rule covers them.

independent_task.brief: Produce a role/unit/function/register/value policy and a parser/authorization test matrix using only synthetic requests.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: All fields and the full register range are checked against the correct role.
TCP stream framing is distinguished from application message boundaries.
Protocol authorization is not represented as independent process-safety certification.

lessons.title: DMZ services, historian exchange and constrained data publishing
lessons.body:
A demilitarized or intermediate service zone provides controlled points where different trust domains exchange required information. Its value comes from the services and restrictions implemented there, not from the zone name. For OT reporting, separate collection from enterprise presentation. A process-side collector can publish an approved data set to an intermediary, and an enterprise-facing service can read that published representation. The enterprise user should not gain arbitrary query or command capability to the original controller merely because a report needs current values.

Choose data direction deliberately. An OT-originated publish session can reduce the need for enterprise-initiated connections into the process zone, but the session remains bidirectional at the transport level and its application permissions matter. A broker, historian replica or file-transfer intermediary should have a narrowly defined role. If the intermediary stores credentials that administer the controller, compromise of the intermediary can still create a control path. Minimize downstream authority and keep management, update and recovery conduits separate from the routine telemetry exchange.

Define the data contract. Identify source assets, approved topics or objects, fields, units, timestamps, quality, sequence identifiers, maximum age and permitted consumers. Validate schema and bounds at appropriate points. A value without its age or quality can be misleading even if the TLS session is authentic. A consumer must distinguish a current measurement, an old retained sample, an estimate and a communication failure. Preserve original source timestamps and make processing/receipt times separate fields so that buffering does not turn stale data into apparently new data.

Constrain application intermediaries. A report service should select from approved data sources through fixed server-side configuration and authorization, not allow an enterprise client to provide an arbitrary internal URL or command. An HTTP reverse proxy forwards application requests; it is not inherently a read-only data diode. Limit methods, paths, parameters, object access and backend credentials according to the actual service. A GET request can still trigger a state-changing backend operation if the application is designed that way, so method filtering alone does not prove read-only semantics.

For message brokers, separate publish and subscribe authority by identity and namespace. A telemetry producer may publish only its own approved topic subtree; a report consumer may subscribe only to the data it needs and must not publish control messages. Wildcards can include future or unrelated topics, so review their scope and topic creation process. Retained messages and durable queues support continuity but require age and quality handling. Authentication of the broker connection does not by itself establish that every topic's payload is valid or appropriate for every subscriber.

Size and monitor queues using arrival and service rates. When arrival exceeds service, backlog grows at their difference. After the burst, recovery depends on spare service capacity, not the total service rate alone. A queue that prevents data loss can still violate freshness requirements if old samples are presented as current. Decide whether the application should preserve every event, aggregate samples, discard obsolete telemetry or signal degraded quality; different data types have different obligations. Never apply a telemetry-discard rule to process commands without a separately justified command protocol and authorization design.

A physical unidirectional mechanism can enforce one-way transfer at its boundary, but applications may require specialized proxies or replication because ordinary bidirectional sessions expect acknowledgments and other return traffic. Verify how the selected supported solution handles delivery evidence, buffering, loss, duplicates and management. The one-way data path does not automatically constrain a separate maintenance connection. Whether using a broker, replica, proxy or one-way device, test the intended data service and attempts to turn the intermediary into an unauthorized command or lateral-access path.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC PUBLISHING DESIGN: Collector O reads controller C and publishes telemetry to DMZ broker D. Enterprise report service W reads D; users reach W over HTTPS. Requirement: enterprise users obtain telemetry no older than2 seconds with original source time/quality; they cannot command C. O's broker identity may publish plant/A/telemetry/# only. W's intended identity is subscribe-only to that subtree, but current ACL allows publish and subscribe to plant/A/#, which includes plant/A/control/. W also accepts a client-supplied backend URL and holds a controller-admin credential for a legacy report function. Queue service capacity is100 messages/s. A60-second burst arrives at150 messages/s from an initially empty queue; normal arrival after the burst is50 messages/s. W currently stamps every dequeued sample with its receipt time and displays good quality.
worked_examples.solution:
The current W design has two paths exceeding report authority. Its broker ACL can publish into the control namespace, and its arbitrary backend selection plus controller-admin credential can originate process-affecting requests. HTTPS protects a transport segment but does not constrain those application capabilities. Use a fixed approved data interface and least-privilege credentials, restrict W to the required subscribe namespace and deny control publication, then test the backend function rather than assuming the HTTP method makes it read-only.

The burst creates (150−100)×60=3,000 queued messages. Once arrival returns to50/s, the queue drains at100−50=50 messages/s, taking60 seconds to clear if rates stay constant. The oldest waiting records can be far beyond the two-second freshness requirement. Replacing source time with receipt time conceals that age and falsely restores good quality. Preserve original timestamps and quality, define consumer behavior for stale records, and select a buffering/aggregation policy compatible with the required telemetry semantics. Queue capacity alone does not solve the freshness requirement.

guided_practice.prompt: Design three negative tests that show W cannot become a controller command path, and one degraded-data test.
guided_practice.hint: Test each authority source: broker permissions, backend selection and credential capability.
guided_practice.solution: Attempt W publication to the control namespace and require denial; submit an unapproved backend target and require rejection before internal access; use W’s deployed backend identity against a state-changing operation and verify it lacks that authority. For degraded data, deliver an authentic sample older than two seconds and verify W preserves original time and indicates/rejects stale quality according to the approved requirement rather than restamping it as current.

independent_task.brief: Produce a DMZ data-flow design, broker permission matrix, data schema and queue/freshness acceptance plan.

lessons.title: Remote maintenance with bounded sessions and target authority
lessons.body:
Remote maintenance should expose the specific engineering function required for an approved task, under an accountable identity and bounded conditions. Begin with the target application, permitted operations, maintenance approval, source-device expectations, timing and recovery needs. Choose a supported remote-access platform that can enforce those requirements and produce evidence. A broad VPN route can be appropriate for some managed workflows, but it grants a different surface from a single application proxy or destination-limited tunnel; the design must explain why the chosen reach is necessary.

The access workflow has several stages: request and approval, enrollment of the named identity/device, authentication, session admission, target authorization, privileged action, monitoring, termination and credential/session cleanup. Tie the stages together with identifiers and trustworthy time. An approval ticket does not technically prevent a session outside the window unless a control enforces it. A valid login does not authorize every target or command. An account expiry does not necessarily terminate sessions or tokens already issued. Test these transitions explicitly.

The following is an unexecuted OpenSSH 9.6+ portable-style teaching fragment for a dedicated forwarding account, using supported syntax that must be checked against the installed release and authentication backend. It is not a complete bastion deployment. The two authentication methods need correctly enabled, independently managed mechanisms; the configuration text alone does not prove a suitable MFA implementation. OpenSSH is used here to teach a narrow transport control, not as a substitute for a full industrial privileged-access system.

```text
PubkeyAuthentication yes
KbdInteractiveAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive
Match User vendor_tunnel
    AllowTcpForwarding local
    PermitOpen 10.130.0.40:443
    MaxSessions 0
    AllowStreamLocalForwarding no
    AllowAgentForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no
    PermitTunnel no
```

The matching account can request local forwarding only to the listed destination/port, while shell/login/subsystem sessions are disallowed by the session setting. These restrictions must be evaluated with the effective configuration and key-level restrictions; a different Match block or authentication route can alter the result. An illustrative client command is `ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:9443:10.130.0.40:443 -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes vendor_tunnel@bastion.example`. The listener is bound to loopback, reducing exposure to other hosts on the client network. Successful forwarding setup does not prove the ultimate HTTPS service works or that its certificate identity and application authorization are correct.

A tunnel does not supply operation-level control at the target. The service on443 may support read reports and administrative changes through the same connection. Use a target role or capable application intermediary to constrain the permitted function and preserve individual attribution. If the target logs only a shared account, correlate it with the named remote session where technically possible, and record any remaining ambiguity. Do not claim that encrypted forwarding automatically records the protected application contents.

Design session lifetime and revocation independently from liveness and inactivity checks. Keepalive mechanisms help detect a dead peer; idle limits respond to lack of activity; a maximum lifetime bounds even an active session. None should be assumed to invalidate all downstream application tokens. The approved termination procedure must address existing transport channels, application authority and reconnect behavior within the specified time, while coordinating any operation that can be left partially complete. Monitor and test the revocation integration after platform or identity changes.

Provide a controlled degraded mode if remote support is required during primary identity failure. Emergency authorization must remain available under the initiating outage, with suitable custody, privilege, recording and post-use cleanup. Avoid creating a permanently open bypass in the name of recovery. Commission the remote path with permitted and forbidden destinations, shell/subsystem attempts, alternative forwarding modes, client-listener exposure, approved-window boundaries, active revocation, target authorization and relevant failure cases. Preserve a site-approved rollback and local control path; no live access is created by the examples in this programme.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC REMOTE-ACCESS RESULTS: Account vendor_tunnel has the reference effective settings. Approved target G=10.130.0.40:443; maintenance window14:00–15:00 UTC. Test A establishes the loopback9443 listener and authenticates, but G's HTTPS service is stopped. Test B requests forwarding to10.130.0.41:443 and is denied. Test C requests a shell and is denied. Test D uses the allowed G tunnel with a target application account that has both ReportRead and ControllerAdmin roles. No session maximum lifetime or window-enforcement integration is configured. At15:05 an active session still works. Directory disablement blocks a new authentication but an existing tunnel and target token remain usable. Target logs show shared_app, while two named vendor tunnel sessions are concurrent. Emergency approval is hosted on the same unavailable identity service.
worked_examples.solution:
A proves setup of the SSH forwarding listener, not health of the destination service; ExitOnForwardFailure does not make every later backend connection successful. B and C are appropriate evidence for destination and shell restrictions in the tested effective configuration. D reveals a separate application-authorization gap: the narrow443 tunnel still exposes ControllerAdmin through the target identity. Replace or restrict that role according to the maintenance requirement.

The session continuing after15:00 shows that the approved window has not been technically bound to the active workflow. Directory disablement does not revoke the existing tunnel or target token in the supplied implementation. Two concurrent named sessions converging on shared_app also leave attribution ambiguous without a reliable operation-to-session mapping. Emergency approval repeats the identity-service dependency it must survive. The complete design therefore needs time/approval enforcement, supported end-to-end revocation, target least privilege, attribution and a controlled independent emergency process in addition to the already demonstrated transport restrictions.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a test sequence for closing the15:00 window that covers existing channels, new authentication and a retained target token.
guided_practice.hint: The protected operation is the final authority to verify; closing one layer may leave another usable.
guided_practice.solution: Before15:00 establish a named authorized session and a harmless target operation. At the defined window-close trigger, invoke the supported session/token revocation workflow. Measure when the old tunnel and target token can no longer perform the protected operation; attempt new authentication and reconnect through the old credentials/session material. Verify denial under the closed window, preserve audit correlation and confirm unrelated approved local control remains functional.

lessons.title: Identity, role design and authorization lifecycle
lessons.body:
Identity design must answer two different questions: who or what is making the request, and whether that principal may perform this operation now. Authentication establishes a claimed identity through supported credentials and trust. Authorization combines that identity with roles, target, operation, approval, operating conditions and explicit restrictions. A valid certificate or successful MFA login is necessary for some workflows but does not by itself grant process-changing authority.

Define roles from actual tasks. A telemetry reader needs the permitted measurements, not engineering download rights. An engineer may need approved setpoint changes; a project maintainer may need controlled logic deployment; a security administrator may manage accounts without changing process logic; an auditor may read evidence without deleting it. The exact separation depends on platform capability and staffing, but document any combined authority and its consequences. Avoid creating a generic administrator role simply because several tasks share one application.

Specify effective-permission semantics. Some systems combine group grants by union, some use more complex precedence, and explicit denies may override grants under defined conditions. Use the actual platform's rules and test nested membership. A user can acquire a powerful role indirectly through a group that appears to be read-oriented. Keep a graph of role/group relationships, reject cycles or ambiguous configurations where the chosen system cannot handle them safely, and evaluate the resulting capability rather than the display name. The synthetic policy below explicitly uses union of grants followed by deny override; it is not a claim that every vendor implements that model.

Bind high-consequence approvals to the action. An approval should identify the actor, target, operation, relevant artifact or value scope, validity interval and accountable approver. A generic ticket saying maintenance approved should not authorize every project download for the rest of the month. For two-person review, distinguish people from account names: two accounts belonging to the same person do not provide independent review. Preserve the approval identity in the audit chain and prevent a requester from altering the approved scope after the decision.

Use short-lived authority where appropriate, but define its evaluation point. A temporary engineering role can expire at a stated time, yet a cached authorization decision or long-lived token may continue to work. Decide whether the expiry is checked at session creation, each protected operation or another supported boundary, and ensure that choice meets the requirement. Revocation latency includes propagation through identity, gateway, application and cache layers. A ten-minute cache cannot meet a thirty-second revocation requirement unless a separate invalidation mechanism reliably updates it.

Service identities need a different workflow from human accounts. A collector can authenticate with a certificate or managed secret and receive narrowly scoped machine permissions without an interactive human MFA prompt on every poll. Protect its private key/secret, prevent unnecessary interactive use, restrict targets and functions, rotate credentials through a validated process and monitor failures. Do not reuse a human administrator account for unattended polling merely to avoid service-account design. Device and service identities must be decommissioned when their asset or function is removed.

Design evidence and recovery together. Record the authenticated principal, effective role decision, approval reference, target/operation, result and trusted time at the relevant enforcement point. Avoid logging secrets. Emergency access needs controlled custody, a supported independent authorization route during primary identity loss and post-use reconciliation/rotation. Test both successful required actions and denied adjacent actions, including nested privilege, explicit deny, expired roles, mismatched approvals, retained tokens and a single person using multiple accounts. The result should be a maintainable authorization model whose actual decisions can be explained and reproduced.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC AUTHORIZATION MODEL: Grants combine by union, then explicit deny overrides. Reader={read}; Engineer={read,setpoint}; ProjectMaintainer={read,download}; Auditor={read_audit}; SecurityAdmin={manage_accounts}. User U has Engineer and Auditor directly and inherits ProjectMaintainer through group Maintenance; U has explicit deny download. Temporary Engineer grant expires at14:30:00, with validity defined as now<expiry and checked on each operation. Separate user V has ProjectMaintainer and no deny. Approval A7 allows V to download project hash h7 to G from14:00 inclusive to14:20 exclusive; approver person_id=P2, requester person_id=P1. Another approval A8 uses two account names both mapped to person_id=P1. Collector S has certificate identity and Reader only, no interactive login. An application caches effective roles for10 minutes; required revocation is≤30 seconds and no push invalidation exists.
worked_examples.solution:
U's inherited ProjectMaintainer role would grant download, but the explicit deny overrides it under the stated synthetic semantics. U can still have other independent grants such as read_audit; denying one operation does not erase every role. At14:30, the temporary Engineer grant is no longer valid because the interval is exclusive at expiry, but other roles must be evaluated separately. A blanket 'user expired' conclusion would be too broad if only one grant expired.

V's A7 approval is valid only for the specified actor, target, operation, artifact and interval. A different project hash or target is not covered. A8 does not supply independent two-person review because both accounts map to P1. S's machine authentication is compatible with a noninteractive reader role when its credentials and lifecycle are controlled; it does not need a human login prompt for each poll. The ten-minute cache cannot meet the thirty-second revocation bound as described. Add supported invalidation or a suitably bounded decision mechanism and test the retained authority through the application, not only directory state.

guided_practice.prompt: Evaluate V downloading h7 to G at14:19:59, at14:20:00, and downloading h8 at14:10. State the differing failed condition where applicable.
guided_practice.hint: Approval time is half-open and the artifact digest is part of the scope.
guided_practice.solution: At14:19:59 the approval conditions are satisfied if authentication and all other required controls are valid. At14:20:00 the approval has expired because the upper bound is exclusive. At14:10 h8 is not covered even though the time is valid, because A7 authorizes h7. Each decision should preserve the actor, approval, target/artifact and reason without exposing credentials.

acceptance_criteria: The stated grant/deny semantics are applied explicitly rather than inferred from names.

lessons.title: PKI, TLS identity and trust-store lifecycle
lessons.body:
Transport encryption is useful only when the application also establishes the intended peer and authorizes its actions. A TLS connection can protect data in transit while connecting to the wrong authenticated server, accepting an overly broad client identity or carrying an unauthorized process command. Define the peer identity expected by the application, the trust anchors allowed to authenticate it, the certificate purpose, the required protocol configuration and the application role assigned after authentication. RFC9846 is the current TLS1.3 specification used for this source review and supersedes RFC8446; a product claiming TLS1.3 support still needs its actual supported implementation and configuration assessed.

Certificate validation involves several related checks. Build an acceptable chain from the leaf through required intermediates to a trusted anchor; validate signatures and applicable constraints; check the validity interval against trustworthy time; verify the intended usage; and compare the application’s expected service identity with the certificate’s supported identity fields. The client should not accept an arbitrary trusted certificate merely because a chain exists. Server Name Indication selects a server context during TLS negotiation, while hostname verification checks the returned identity; setting one is not a substitute for the other.

The following commands are unexecuted OpenSSL3.0 teaching examples using synthetic files and addresses. They illustrate inspection, offline validation and an explicitly verifying client test. Do not run a network test against live equipment without the appropriate authorization and supported test plan.

```text
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl verify -CAfile roots.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem -purpose sslserver -verify_hostname g.ot.example leaf.pem
openssl s_client -connect 10.130.0.40:443 -servername g.ot.example -verify_hostname g.ot.example -verify_return_error -CAfile roots.pem
```

The offline command evaluates the supplied certificate material and expected name; it does not prove that the running server presents that leaf or possesses the matching private key. The client test addresses the deployed peer and is configured to fail on verification errors, but still does not prove the application role is correct. An inspection command prints fields without making every trust decision. Preserve the distinction among displaying a certificate, validating a file, completing an authenticated handshake and exercising an authorized application operation.

Mutual TLS authenticates clients as well as servers when correctly configured. Map each accepted client identity to a bounded role rather than treating every certificate from a large corporate CA as an OT administrator. Validate the supported certificate purpose and issuer/namespace policy, and protect private keys in an appropriate supported store. A certificate file is public identity material; the private key enables proof of possession and must not be embedded in source code, reports or broadly readable backups. A signed certificate does not prove the key has never been copied.

Plan trust changes as operational changes. Renewal requires issuance, delivery, key/certificate matching, peer-chain compatibility, activation and validation before expiry. During a planned CA transition, a bounded overlap can let peers move from old to new trust, but every relying party and rollback condition must be tracked. Retaining obsolete or compromised anchors indefinitely broadens trust. Removing an old anchor before dependent peers migrate can interrupt service. Test the transition on representative clients, including those with limited embedded trust stores or unusual chain handling.

Revocation and time failure need explicit policy. An offline OT client may not reach an online status responder; determine whether it uses a maintained revocation list, short-lived credentials, controlled trust-store updates or another supported design. State what happens when status evidence is unavailable and what residual exposure is accepted. Do not silently disable all validation to restore connectivity. Clock error can make a valid certificate appear expired or not yet valid, so time health and recovery belong in the trust design.

Finally, preserve application semantics. TLS session resumption and early data have their own replay and lifecycle considerations; do not use replayable early data for non-idempotent process changes without an application design that meets the requirement. Certificate revocation may not terminate an existing application session automatically. Test wrong names, untrusted issuers, expired/not-yet-valid material, wrong purpose, missing intermediates, key mismatch, renewal overlap, status-service loss and retained sessions. Pair each rejection with required service continuity and a controlled recovery procedure so that trust remains both meaningful and operable.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC CERTIFICATE/SESSION CASE, assessment time2026-09-19T12:00Z: Expected server identity g.ot.example; allowed root SiteRootA. L1 chains to SiteRootA, has serverAuth purpose, SAN g.ot.example, and has a validity interval from 2026-09-01T00:00Z through 2026-09-20T12:00Z. L2 chains to SiteRootA and has serverAuth but SAN g-backup.ot.example. L3 has SAN g.ot.example and serverAuth but chains only to untrusted CorpRootB. L4 is presented as a client certificate but has only serverAuth purpose; client policy requires clientAuth. The running server has a private key that does not match L1. One client clock is48 hours fast. A proposed root rotation removes SiteRootA before two embedded clients receive the new root. An offline client cannot reach its online revocation responder; no approved failure policy exists. A process-change API is proposed for TLS early data without application replay handling.
worked_examples.solution:
L1's supplied certificate fields fit the offline server checks at the stated assessment time, but the running server's mismatched private key prevents a valid proof-of-possession handshake using that leaf. L2 fails the expected name despite a trusted chain; L3 fails the allowed trust-anchor policy despite the correct name. L4 fails the stated client-purpose requirement. These are different failures and require different corrections rather than a single instruction to disable certificate checking.

The fast client believes the time is2026-09-21T12:00Z and can reject L1 as expired even though it has24 hours remaining at the true assessment time. Correct and validate time through the approved workflow; do not extend trust blindly. Root removal before client migration risks an avoidable service interruption. Revocation-status unavailability needs a deliberate bounded policy and operational treatment, not an implicit pass. The proposed early-data process API also needs replay-safe application semantics or early data disabled for those changes. A successful encrypted connection alone would not resolve these identity and command-lifecycle requirements.

guided_practice.prompt: Design a CA-renewal acceptance plan for the two embedded clients, including a rollback condition that does not restore a known-compromised anchor.
guided_practice.hint: Track each relying party and distinguish routine rotation from compromise response.
guided_practice.solution: Inventory client trust and supported chain formats; stage the approved new anchor/certificate chain; validate correct-name/purpose handshakes and required application function on each client; use a bounded overlap only if the old anchor remains trusted under the risk decision; then remove the old anchor after all required peers have migrated and verify rejection. Define recovery through a trusted alternate issuance/installation process if the old anchor is compromised, rather than automatically re-enabling it to regain connectivity.

independent_task.brief: Produce a certificate trust matrix and a representative renewal/revocation test plan with explicit identity, purpose, time and application-role checks.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Trusted chain, expected identity, purpose and key possession are separate checks.
Renewal and root rotation preserve required service without indefinite excess trust.
Unavailable revocation evidence and replay-sensitive operations have explicit supported policies.
