lessons.title: Host hardening that preserves the required OT service
lessons.body:
Host hardening reduces unnecessary capability while preserving required functions. Begin with the host's actual role and dependencies, not a generic desktop checklist. An engineering workstation, historian, HMI server and database host need different services, rights and communication paths. Identify operating-system and application versions, installed packages, listening services, scheduled tasks, startup components, local accounts, filesystem permissions and remote-management mechanisms. Record which items are required, who owns them and what evidence supports that decision. An undocumented service is a question to resolve, not automatic permission to remove it during operation.

Translate the cybersecurity requirements specification into a supported baseline. Disable or remove unnecessary services and default accounts, restrict required listeners to appropriate interfaces and sources, protect administrative access, apply least privilege to service identities and maintain audit/time configuration. A listener bound to every interface may expose an otherwise approved service on an unintended network. A host firewall can narrow source, destination and service paths, but its effectiveness depends on profile selection, rule precedence, management access and actual application behaviour. Test both required communication and adjacent prohibited paths.

Privilege has several forms. A service running as a powerful system account can modify more than its application data even if its network account appears read-only. Review local filesystem, registry/configuration, service-control and credential access under the selected operating system. Conversely, removing all write permission may stop the application maintaining its database or queue. Assign the minimum supported rights to the exact directories and functions, and verify normal operation, restart, upgrade and restore. Inherited directory rights and writable executable locations can undermine an otherwise narrow role.

Patching and security agents are engineering changes. Obtain the selected vendor's compatibility position, representative test environment, baseline backup and rollback method. Exercise the workload, controller communications, alarms, history and recovery while measuring latency, resource consumption and failure behaviour. A scan that is harmless on an office computer can interfere with time-sensitive software or unsupported legacy components. Use a justified maintenance schedule and bounded configuration; do not install every available agent simply to increase the number of controls. Unsupported or temporarily deferred measures need a risk disposition, compensating controls, owner and review date.

Antimalware exclusions require precise scope. Excluding a high-write database directory may be justified after validation; excluding an entire drive or all engineering file types can create a large unexamined execution path. Document what is excluded, why, how integrity is checked elsewhere and how the exception is reviewed. Application control and removable-media handling add different protections and are developed in the next chapter. One control should not be represented as proving every property of a host.

Protect the boot and recovery chain using supported platform features. Secure boot, disk encryption and trusted recovery media can contribute to integrity or confidentiality, but compatibility and key recovery matter. Encryption whose recovery key is available only on the failed host can make an outage unrecoverable. A known-good image must include the supported operating system, application, drivers, security settings and references to separately restored data and credentials. Its digest proves correspondence to recorded bytes; approval and provenance establish whether those bytes are the intended baseline.

Hardening must survive lifecycle events. Compare effective settings after reboot, domain/group-policy application, vendor maintenance and restoration. A manually closed port that reopens at the next service restart is not a durable control. Detect drift using an approved baseline and explain exceptions. Avoid treating every difference as malicious: a vendor update may legitimately add a service, but its purpose, exposure and compatibility require review before accepting the new baseline.

Acceptance includes service continuity and security outcomes. Required collector reads succeed; unauthorised management and unnecessary listeners fail; service identities cannot modify executable directories beyond their role; audit records reach the intended collector; and restore re-establishes both function and hardening. Record the exact host/version/workload and untested conditions. These are original design exercises informed by public systems/OT engineering guidance, not a reproduction of licensed standard clauses or proof of an achieved security level.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — HOST H1 (synthetic historian): supported application version7 on a vendor-approved OS build. Required services: collector TCP4840 client to C1, database TCP5432 client to DB1, time and audit to approved servers, administration only through J1. Unused file-sharing service listens on all interfaces. Collector runs as local administrator and writes C:/PlantData/queue; C:/PlantApp/bin is also writable by that account. A proposed antimalware exclusion covers all of C:. A representative workload has a required maximum observation-processing interval of100ms; baseline measured worst case70ms, proposed full scan adds a measured45ms under the same test. Required audit-loss detection≤60s; proposed log-buffer alarm triggers at300s. Approved restore image digest is h11; a candidate image has h12 with no change record. Disk encryption recovery key is stored only on H1. A manual firewall restriction disappears after policy refresh. No production changes are authorised by this exercise.
worked_examples.solution:
H1 needs a role-specific baseline. Remove or restrict the unused sharing service through the approved compatibility/change process. Constrain collector traffic to C1 and database traffic to DB1 while preserving time, audit and J1 administration. Replace unnecessary local-administrator execution with supported least privilege; allow the required queue writes while preventing unauthorised changes to executable code. Narrow and justify the antimalware exception rather than excluding the whole drive.

The measured processing interval becomes115ms under the supplied additive test result, exceeding100ms; a different supported scan schedule/configuration or other mitigation requires validation. The300s audit-loss alarm fails the60s requirement. h12 is not the approved h11 baseline without a reviewed change and applicable tests. Recoverable key custody must survive H1 loss. The firewall restriction must be implemented in the effective policy source so it persists after refresh, then tested from permitted and prohibited origins. None of these observations alone determines full standard conformance.

guided_practice.prompt: Specify the service identity and filesystem changes for H1, then identify normal, restart and negative tests that would prove the intended rights without breaking queue operation.
guided_practice.hint: Separate the directory that must receive data from the directory containing executable code, and verify effective permissions rather than account labels.
guided_practice.solution: Use a supported non-administrative service identity with the minimum queue/configuration rights. Remove unnecessary write access to C:/PlantApp/bin, verify normal queue creation and restart recovery, attempt an unauthorised executable modification in the isolated test, and confirm the effective rights after policy refresh. Preserve a tested rollback and vendor compatibility evidence.

lessons.title: Application control and removable-media transfer design
lessons.body:
Application control constrains what may execute and under which conditions. It differs from malware detection: an unknown program may be undesirable even when no signature identifies it as malicious. Conversely, an approved program can be abused or contain a vulnerability. Define the protected host role, allowed software, scripts, libraries, installers and maintenance tools from the operational requirement. Determine what the selected product actually controls; executable files, script interpreters, dynamically loaded libraries and macros may follow different enforcement paths.

Rule design determines both assurance and maintenance burden. A hash rule identifies exact bytes and therefore changes when the artifact changes. A publisher/signature rule can permit a controlled set of signed releases but needs a trusted signing identity, relevant product/version constraints and revocation/update handling. A path rule trusts a location; if unprivileged users can write there, they may introduce new content that inherits the location's permission. Protect the directory and its parent/installation workflow, or choose a more suitable rule. A policy label saying approved is not evidence of the effective match conditions.

Use staged deployment. Begin in an isolated representative environment, identify required execution paths and review audit observations. Audit-only mode records a would-be decision but does not enforce denial. Move to enforcement only after needed software and lifecycle operations are covered, with recovery and an authorised exception route. Do not convert every audit event into a permanent allow rule; a learning period can observe unwanted activity as well as legitimate work. Negative tests should verify that adjacent unapproved artifacts are blocked while required functions continue.

Updates require a promotion workflow. Obtain an artifact from an approved origin, validate integrity and applicable signature/trust, check version and compatibility, test the required workload and rollback, approve the exact release and update the policy coherently. A hash change is not proof of malware, but it invalidates an exact-hash match. A valid signature identifies a signer under the trust model; it does not prove the release is free of vulnerabilities or approved for this host. Preserve the source, digest, verification result, test record and approval link.

Removable media crosses a trust boundary even when the destination has no Internet connection. Specify who may use media, approved devices and purposes, custody, preparation, transfer station, content inspection, destination controls and evidence. Encryption protects confidentiality when media is lost; it does not remove malicious content. Disabling autorun reduces one execution path but does not stop an operator manually launching an unapproved file. A device identifier or label supports inventory but is not by itself a strong guarantee of content or device authenticity.

Transfer should preserve artifact identity from approval to use. Scan or inspect the exact extracted content under the supported process, validate its digest/signature, copy through the controlled route and verify the destination bytes before execution. Archives may contain nested or password-protected material that the inspection tool cannot examine. Treat that as incomplete inspection, not a clean result. Obtain an inspectable approved package or use an explicitly reviewed alternative. The transfer station itself needs hardening, updates, isolation and audit; a compromised inspection machine can invalidate the trust chain.

Exceptions must be narrower than the emergency. Bind a temporary allowance to the actor or role, host, artifact, purpose, validity interval and approved operation. A broad folder exception without expiry can outlive the maintenance task. Define whether running processes or cached policy retain authority after expiry, and test the actual product behaviour. Record removal and post-work verification, including policy state, unexpected files and restored normal operation. The workflow should support recovery without depending on an unrestricted permanent bypass.

Assess the entire sequence rather than a single product result. An approved tool copied correctly can still be executed with excessive privilege or used against an unauthorised controller. Application control, identity, process permission and change authority are complementary. This chapter's exact matching and interval rules are explicit synthetic assumptions, not universal vendor semantics. The independent task produces a policy and acceptance design; actual enforcement, device behaviour and supported update testing remain selected-platform work under the appropriate authority.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — TRANSFER CASE (synthetic): Engineering host E1 allows exact hash a12 for ToolA and a publisher rule limited to VendorV/ProductB/version4. A path rule allows C:/ApprovedTools/*, but ordinary maintenance users can write that directory. Proposed ToolA update has hash b12, valid VendorV signature and version5; E1 compatibility testing covers only ToolA's previous release. Media M1 is encrypted and contains b12 plus an unrelated unsigned script. Transfer station T1 reports the password-protected archive unscanned; the operator calls the overall package clean. Destination E1 copy of ToolA has hash c12. A temporary exception X allows technician U to run hash b12 on E1 from10:00 inclusive to10:30 exclusive, with policy defined to check each new process launch. Application-control deployment is still audit-only. A proposed emergency bypass allows all files on every engineering host indefinitely. No actual executable or malware is supplied.
worked_examples.solution:
The writable path rule creates a way for unapproved content to gain execution permission by location. Protect and validate the path or replace the rule with suitable supported matching. b12 does not match the exact a12 rule; its signature alone neither establishes E1 compatibility nor makes it match the separately constrained ProductB/version4 rule. The destination digest c12 fails the approved-artifact identity check and requires investigation before execution.

Encrypted M1 protects data confidentiality but does not make the script or archive safe. The unscanned archive is an inspection gap. Audit-only mode cannot prove blocking. Under X's explicit model, a new b12 launch at10:29 is in scope if all other conditions hold; at10:30 it is outside the interval. The exception does not cover c12, another user or another host. Replace the indefinite bypass with a reviewed bounded exception and test enforcement, expiry and restoration. Do not claim these checks alone prove the tool's process action authorised.

guided_practice.prompt: Build a decision table for launching a12, b12 and c12 from the writable approved-tools path, separating the current unsafe rule set from the intended corrected policy.
guided_practice.hint: Evaluate each rule independently and distinguish exact content identity, location trust, publisher scope and temporary exception conditions.
guided_practice.solution: The current path allowance can permit content simply by placement, undermining the narrow hash policy. In the corrected design, protect/remove that path rule and evaluate exact approved hashes or constrained publisher rules plus authorised exceptions. b12 requires validated promotion or a properly scoped exception; c12 fails the approved b12 identity and must not inherit permission merely from the directory name. Record actual vendor precedence and enforce negative tests.

independent_task.brief: Create an application-control and media-transfer specification with a rule table, artifact promotion record, bounded exception and acceptance tests.

A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Writable paths, scripts/libraries and audit-versus-enforcement behaviour are explicitly assessed.
Artifact identity is verified across origin, inspection, transfer and destination.
Unscanned content and expired or out-of-scope exceptions cannot be reported as approved.

lessons.title: Legacy controllers, serial gateways and compensating controls
lessons.body:
Legacy constraints do not remove a system from the cybersecurity design. They change where controls can be enforced and which risks remain. A serial controller may lack user accounts, cryptographic authentication, signed updates or detailed audit. A gateway can provide a controlled IP-facing path, but it cannot retroactively make the downstream protocol authenticate every device. Describe the complete path from human or service principal through host, gateway, serial bus and endpoint, including physical access and maintenance connectors.

Separate addressing, integrity checking and authentication. A serial unit address selects a responding device; it is not proof of a trustworthy identity. A frame CRC detects certain transmission errors; it does not identify an authorised sender or prevent a knowledgeable sender producing a valid frame. A good response also does not establish correct register interpretation or physical measurement. The design needs the exact device map, function support, serial settings, quality/freshness handling and relevant process permissions in addition to transport access.

Restrict the IP-facing gateway to required peers and services. If reads and writes share the same TCP port, a port-only firewall rule cannot distinguish them. A supported protocol-aware enforcement point may restrict functions or data ranges, but only if it correctly parses the selected implementation and actually lies on every relevant path. Encrypted or proprietary tunnelling can change what an intermediate device can inspect. If function enforcement is unavailable, constrain the initiating application and its privileges, network reach and maintenance workflow, while explicitly recording the remaining capability.

Gateway configuration is itself privileged. An administrator who can change downstream mappings, enable a tunnel or alter serial settings can affect the controlled boundary. Protect its management interface, credentials, firmware/configuration provenance and backup/restore. Limit simultaneous clients and connection behaviour according to vendor support and validated bus capacity. A gateway accepting many IP clients can serialize them onto one slow serial channel; throughput and timeout behaviour become an availability dependency.

Serial timing is a shared resource. Calculate wire time from bytes, bits per character and baud rate, then add turnaround, processing, required gaps and retry/timeout behaviour. A nonresponding device can dominate a polling cycle when each request waits for a long timeout. Security inspection or extra monitoring polls must be included in the performance budget. A passive observation design is often preferable for initial visibility, but electrical loading, capture location and tool behaviour still require review; merely naming a tool passive does not prove it cannot disturb the bus.

Protect direct physical and maintenance paths. A laptop attached downstream of the gateway may bypass the IP firewall and function filter entirely. Control cabinet access, service ports, approved maintenance equipment and the work procedure accordingly. A locked room reduces opportunity but does not provide protocol authentication or eliminate authorised-insider misuse. Account for temporary connections and restore the normal boundary after work. Do not disable independent local protection to simplify a gateway test.

Freshness and failure behaviour connect cybersecurity to operation. A gateway may return cached values while the serial device is unavailable. Preserve acquisition age and source status, and define which actions require current evidence. A TCP session that remains connected is not proof the downstream process is observed. Decide how gateway loss, deny actions, overload and restart affect local control, alarms and operator access. A generic fail-open or fail-closed label is incomplete: identify which communication or control function changes and its process consequence.

Compensating measures need an assurance argument. State the missing capability, threat path, alternative controls, tested effectiveness, operational limitations and residual risk owner. A network enclosure does not magically award the endpoint a security capability it lacks. Review exceptions periodically and plan supported replacement, spares, backup and migration. Test restored gateway mappings and serial settings as well as IP reachability. The synthetic calculations below support design reasoning; actual bus wiring, protocol-aware enforcement and process consequences require selected-platform and supervised evidence.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — LEGACY CELL (synthetic): Reader R and maintainer M reach gateway G on TCP502. G translates to a single9600bit/s ModbusRTU bus with11bits per character. Device D7 supports reads and writes without authentication. The firewall permits R and M to G:502; it cannot parse function codes. A proposed G function filter would allow R reads only, but its support for this firmware is unverified. A downstream maintenance socket permits direct serial attachment. Normal transaction:8-byte request,9-byte response,10ms processing and two4ms gaps. Ten devices are polled sequentially. A missing device uses500ms timeout per attempt with two total attempts. G's IP session remains up while its cached D7 source value is30s old; restart permission requires source age≤2s. G configuration backup records9600baud/unit7, but a replacement is set19200baud/unit1. Local protective logic continues independently of G; settings changes require the electrical/process authority.
worked_examples.solution:
The firewall limits peers and port but cannot distinguish R reads from writes on the shared service. The proposed protocol filter is a candidate control until supported parsing and actual enforcement are verified. Direct serial attachment bypasses that IP path and requires a separate physical/maintenance boundary. D7's address and CRC do not authenticate an actor.

Normal transaction time is17×11/9600=19.479ms wire time plus18ms processing/gaps, or37.479ms. Ten successful transactions take about374.79ms under this simplified budget. A missing device's two500ms waits add roughly1s of waiting, with any request serialization and other overhead separately accounted. G's30s-old cached value fails the2s restart rule despite TCP connectivity. Restore must correct serial settings and mapping, then prove fresh point semantics and allowed/denied actions. Preserve independent local protection throughout; none of these measures proves a new endpoint security level.

guided_practice.prompt: Design two negative tests: one targeting R attempting a write through G, and one targeting the direct maintenance socket. State what each test can and cannot prove.
guided_practice.hint: A port rule sees transport endpoints; a downstream physical connection may not traverse that rule at all.
guided_practice.solution: In an isolated authorised setup, verify the supported function-control mechanism rejects an R write while required reads still work and evidence reaches the audit path. Separately verify access/custody and maintenance controls for the downstream connector; an IP firewall result cannot prove that direct serial path is controlled. Record actual device compatibility, timing and residual lack of endpoint authentication.

independent_task.brief: Produce a legacy-cell control specification with path/authority map, function enforcement, bus timing, cache/failure policy, physical maintenance boundary and restoration tests.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Unit address and CRC are not represented as authentication.
Port-only, protocol-aware and direct-serial paths have distinct controls and evidence.
Bus timing, stale values and restored device semantics are validated without defeating local protection.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Secure development, integration artifacts and release integrity
lessons.body:
Secure development applies to the software and configuration actually created or modified in the system. An integrator may develop PLC logic, HMI projects, scripts, API clients, database queries, firewall templates and deployment automation while using supported vendor platforms. This does not require inventing a new PLC runtime or rebuilding the vendor's product. Define responsibility for supplier product assurance, integrator-created components, configuration and operational change. Supplier evidence informs selection and review; it does not automatically prove that the assembled application meets its requirements.

Begin with explicit requirements and abuse/failure cases. A telemetry API may require read-only access to approved assets, bounded query ranges, typed results, preserved quality/time and rejection of unauthorised writes. Derive design constraints and tests from those statements. Input validation should reject incompatible types, ranges, identifiers and schemas rather than silently coercing them into plausible process values. Parameterised database operations keep supplied values separate from query structure. Authentication, authorisation and process checks remain necessary after parsing succeeds.

Version all inputs that affect a release. Source revision alone may be insufficient when dependencies, compiler/toolchain, generated configuration, build flags or target firmware change. A release manifest should identify source/configuration revisions, dependency versions, toolchain, target/platform assumptions, artifact digest, test results, approvers and installation/rollback instructions. The exact fields depend on the supported build process. Where reproducible builds are a goal, compare outputs under a controlled environment and investigate differences; a reproducible defect remains a defect.

Review source and configuration for the intended boundary. Look for uncontrolled targets, embedded credentials, excessive privileges, unsafe defaults, missing timeouts, unbounded loops, unchecked conversions and loss of quality/provenance. Static analysis and peer review reveal some defects; tests reveal others. A successful compile establishes that the tool accepted the source, not that units, logic priorities, process permissions or recovery behaviour are correct. Test positive and negative cases, boundary values, partial failure, retry identity, restart and compatibility on the selected supported platform.

Dependencies are part of the delivered system. An inventory or software bill of materials should identify direct and relevant transitive components and versions, with enough context to assess an advisory. A vulnerability identifier alone does not establish exploitability or operational impact in this configuration; neither does a supplier statement of no known vulnerabilities prove absence. Evaluate affected version, reachable function, configuration, exposure, consequence and available mitigations. Track unsupported components and remediation decisions through the release lifecycle instead of losing them inside an archive.

Artifact integrity has several distinct layers. A digest detects a difference from a recorded byte sequence. A digital signature binds signed content to a key under a trust and verification model. Neither proves that the signer was authorised to approve this release, that the key was uncompromised, or that the artifact is appropriate for the target. Verify the expected signing identity and trust chain, signature scope, current policy and the approved release manifest. Protect signing keys and build credentials from routine developer or log access; rotate/revoke them through a supported incident and continuity plan.

Promotion must preserve the exact approved artifact. If tests run on build B1 but deployment uses B2, the test result needs an applicability argument or retest. Rebuilding from the same source with a different library can produce materially different behaviour. Avoid a time-of-check/time-of-use gap in which a mutable download location changes after approval. Bind deployment to immutable identity or a verified digest and target scope, then verify the installed version. Keep secrets out of source, artifact metadata and logs; redact or reference controlled secret storage without erasing useful decision evidence.

Release and rollback include data and external state. A database migration may make the previous application incompatible; restoring old binaries alone may not reverse the schema or external work-order events. Define supported forward/rollback procedures, backup consistency, reconciliation and postconditions. After deployment, verify required functions and denied actions, not merely process startup. Record defects, residual risks and the operational handoff. This chapter supplies an original integration workflow; normative development-process conformance and vendor product certification require their separate applicable evidence and licensed references.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — RELEASE R14 (synthetic): requirement API-1 permits read_history for assets A1/A2 with window≤3600s; writes are prohibited. Source commit s14 was tested with library L=2.1 and toolchain T=4.0 for controller firmware F=3.2, producing artifact digest h14. Test record TR14 includes schema/range/retry and denied-write tests. Deployment package DP14 is rebuilt from s14 with L=2.2 and has digest h15; no new tests exist. The package is signed by key K2, while the approved release policy trusts only K1 for this product. A manifest lists direct library L but omits its bundled parser P=1.7. An advisory affects P1.7 only when optional expression evaluation is enabled; current configuration is unknown. CI logs contain a service token. The application migration changes database schema v5→v6; rollback instructions only copy old application binaries. An example request asks read_history(A1,7200s), and another uses a text asset field containing SQL-like characters. No actual source exploit or credential is supplied.
worked_examples.solution:
DP14 is not the tested artifact: h15 differs from h14 and its dependency changed. The signature must be evaluated against policy; a mathematically valid K2 signature does not satisfy the stated K1 trust requirement. Obtain a reviewed release manifest and applicable tests for the exact deployment artifact/target before promotion. Complete the dependency inventory with P1.7, then determine expression-evaluation configuration and exposure before concluding the advisory applies or is harmless.

The7200s request exceeds API-1's3600s bound and should be rejected or handled by an explicitly approved bounded interface, not silently executed. Asset text must be validated against the allowlist and passed as a parameter rather than query syntax. Revoke/rotate the exposed token under the incident process and remove the secret from future logs while preserving controlled evidence. Rollback needs database compatibility/restoration and external-state reconciliation; old binaries alone are not a complete plan after v6 migration.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a release admission decision for DP14 with separate outcomes for artifact identity, signature policy, dependency advisory, API bounds, credential exposure and rollback readiness.
guided_practice.hint: A single green compile or signature result cannot answer every assurance question; each requirement needs its own evidence.
guided_practice.solution: Hold promotion because DP14 differs from the tested build, uses an unapproved signing key and lacks a complete rollback plan. Resolve P1.7 configuration/exposure before risk disposition. Enforce the asset/window/read-only API requirements with explicit negative tests. Treat the logged token as exposed under the applicable incident procedure. Reissue a manifest binding the exact tested artifact, dependencies, target, approval and recovery steps.

independent_task.brief: Produce a secure integration release package for the synthetic API and deployment, including traceability, dependency/advisory analysis, artifact verification and migration-aware rollback.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Source, dependency, toolchain, target and artifact identities are traceable to applicable tests and approval.
Signature validity, trusted signer, content integrity and functional suitability remain distinct.
Inputs, secrets, partial failure and database rollback have explicit verified handling.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Monitoring placement, visibility and intrusion-detection acceptance
lessons.body:
Monitoring design begins with the decisions it must support. Identify the events and changes that matter: unauthorised engineering access, unexpected writes, new devices, configuration changes, lost telemetry, time degradation or abnormal service use. Map each question to evidence available at an endpoint, network observation point or application. A sensor placed at a convenient uplink may miss local traffic within a switch or another routing path. Coverage is a property of topology, collection configuration and data semantics, not the number of monitoring products installed.

Distinguish collection methods. A switch mirror copies selected traffic subject to platform support, direction, filters and capacity. A network TAP has its own physical and availability characteristics. A packet broker can combine, filter and distribute copies; it does not guarantee complete capture or unlimited bandwidth. Record where observations are taken, what directions and VLANs are included, whether duplicates are present and how drops are measured. A failover path can move traffic away from the original observation point. Verify visibility in normal, maintenance and degraded states.

Capacity limits affect conclusions. If sustained selected input exceeds the output link and buffering cannot absorb the excess indefinitely, some traffic must be dropped or deliberately filtered. A capture file containing no prohibited command is weak evidence when relevant packets may have been omitted. Use drop counters, source sequence evidence and controlled test events to estimate coverage. Avoid treating average throughput as proof that bursts never overflow buffers. Time resolution, timestamp source and synchronisation quality also constrain event correlation.

Passive intrusion detection observes and alerts; inline prevention can interrupt traffic. Do not credit a passive sensor with blocking an operation. Introducing an inline control adds latency, failure and bypass decisions that require process-aware validation. A fail-open bypass may preserve connectivity while losing enforcement; a fail-closed response may remove a needed service. State the exact behaviour and consequence instead of calling either universally safe. Detection and protective process functions remain separate responsibilities.

Detection logic can use known signatures, protocol/state rules or behavioural baselines. Signatures can identify known patterns but may miss novel or differently encoded events. An anomaly can reflect a legitimate maintenance task or an actual threat; context and investigation determine meaning. A learning baseline built during abnormal activity can normalise the wrong behaviour. Record the baseline period, approved maintenance, device identities and expected flows. Tune alerts with evidence rather than disabling an entire category because it is noisy.

Encrypted communication changes visibility. A network sensor may observe endpoints, timing, volume and handshake metadata without seeing protected application operations. Endpoint or application audit can supply complementary evidence. Do not claim deep command inspection when payloads are unavailable, and do not remove necessary encryption merely to make a dashboard decode traffic. If decryption or an application proxy is proposed, assess its trust, key custody, compatibility, performance and operational consequences through the approved design.

Logs and counters need their own integrity and coverage. Preserve source identity, source time, collector receipt time, quality and relevant sequence/discontinuity information. A reset counter can resemble wrap; a collector outage can hide events. Central logging should detect missing sources and buffering failure within the stated requirement. Protect audit access and avoid collecting unnecessary secrets. Retrieved log text remains data; neither automation nor an AI assistant should execute instructions embedded in it.

Acceptance tests follow the intended detection and response chain. Generate a harmless approved representative event in an isolated or supervised environment, verify it is visible at the selected point, parsed correctly, detected, routed to the responsible operator and recorded with useful context. Include a benign adjacent event to test specificity, missing-source and overload cases to test coverage alarms, and failover to test alternate paths. Record false positives, missed detections and response timing without claiming one test proves all future detection. Monitoring is complete only to the extent of its stated, tested scope; actual platform deployment and site operation remain required evidence.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — MONITORING DESIGN (synthetic): Sensor S1 receives a mirror of firewall F's enterprise-facing interface. Controller C1 and engineering workstation E1 communicate within the same downstream VLAN, so their local traffic does not cross F. A backup route through F2 bypasses S1's observation point. Broker B receives sustained selected copies of0.7Gb/s and0.6Gb/s and has one1.0Gb/s output; assume no compression/filtering, finite buffering and the same measurement basis. Required source coverage includes50assets; only47 report, including none of the three critical gateway logs. S1 is passive IDS; a proposal credits it with blocking writes. TLS protects one application flow and S1 has no decryption. Event A source time12:00:00±2s; event B12:00:01±2s. Required alert delivery≤30s; observed detection5s plus routing/notification40s. A maintenance window legitimately changes a device configuration, while the proposed tuning disables all configuration-change alerts indefinitely. No attack traffic or production fault injection is authorised by the exercise.
worked_examples.solution:
S1 cannot observe E1-to-C1 local exchanges or the F2 path merely because it sees F's uplink. Add appropriate supported observation or endpoint evidence and test the relevant normal/failover routes. Broker input totals1.3Gb/s, exceeding output by0.3Gb/s. With sustained input and finite buffering, at least about23.08% of the selected input rate cannot be carried on that output under the stated no-filter/no-compression assumptions; actual packet distribution and burst loss require measurement.

Asset reporting is47/50=94%, but the three missing critical gateways may be more significant than the percentage suggests. Passive S1 detects rather than blocks. TLS limits payload visibility, so use appropriate complementary application evidence. A/B uncertainty intervals overlap, preventing a definite order from timestamps alone. End-to-end alert time is45s, failing30s despite detection in5s. Replace blanket permanent suppression with a scoped maintenance exception and post-window verification, preserving useful audit evidence.

guided_practice.prompt: Redesign the observation plan for the local E1–C1 path and F2 failover, then specify one permitted test event and the evidence needed to prove collection, detection and notification.
guided_practice.hint: Trace the actual packet or application-event path before choosing a sensor location; test the operator notification separately from detection.
guided_practice.solution: Use a supported downstream observation point or endpoint/application audit for local traffic, and cover or collect evidence from F2 during failover. Record direction, VLAN/filter, drop and timestamp assumptions. Generate an approved harmless representative event, verify raw visibility and parsing, confirm the intended alert and operator route within30s, and include a benign comparison plus missing-source test. Do not label the passive sensor a blocker.

independent_task.brief: Produce a monitoring architecture, coverage/capacity analysis and detection acceptance plan including normal, encrypted, overloaded and failover conditions.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Actual local and alternate paths determine collection placement.
Drops, encryption, missing sources and clock uncertainty limit conclusions explicitly.
Detection, blocking and operator response are separately described and tested.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Intrusion detection implementation, evidence and controlled tuning
lessons.body:
## Convert a risk scenario into a detectable claim
A useful detection begins with a specific event and a reason it matters. “Suspicious OT traffic” is not an adequate test oracle. A requirement might identify an unauthorised historian-originated write to a named gateway, including the requested function, target point and operating conditions. Decide which observations can establish each part. A transport connection can establish that two endpoints exchanged packets; it cannot by itself show that a write occurred, that the command was authorised, or that the physical process changed. Link the detection to an independently maintained asset/point map and an accountable response.

Define the observable population. A passive sensor on one switch mirror may see the primary path but miss a service laptop, cellular path or local serial bus. A network sensor can also see encrypted transport while lacking the application plaintext. That is a visibility constraint, not proof that the session is harmless. Consider approved endpoint, application or gateway evidence where it can expose the necessary semantics without undermining the security or availability design. Keep an explicit coverage matrix for paths, directions, protocols, encryption states and normal/failover modes.

## Build a bounded offline implementation
Use an approved isolated workstation and a supported IDS package. Record the exact engine/build, configuration, rule files, enabled protocol parsers and input-capture digest. Pin the lesson to the Suricata 8.0.2 documentation; select the actual supported release for the learner's lab rather than treating a development documentation branch as production guidance. Start with a synthetic PCAP and ordinary unprivileged file access. Do not attach a live OT interface or replay generated traffic onto equipment as part of this offline exercise.

The following independently written rule deliberately detects a transport event, not an industrial write:

```text
alert tcp 10.20.0.10 any -> 10.30.0.40 502 (msg:"Teaching historian connection"; flags:S; sid:1000034; rev:1;)
```

Its header constrains source, destination and destination port. The flag condition selects a SYN pattern. It will not distinguish a subsequent read from a write, and retransmissions can create repeated observations. The message is a human label; naming it “dangerous write” would not add application semantics. Maintain unique rule identifiers and revisions so an alert can be traced to the actual rule baseline. A supported application-aware rule needs the correct parser, direction, decoded operation and relevant point/authorisation context.

A learner with Suricata installed can create an empty output directory and use the following commands against their own approved local files. These commands are documented exercises and were not executed in this build:

```bash
suricata -V
suricata -T -c suricata.yaml -S teaching.rules
suricata -r synthetic.pcap -c suricata.yaml -S teaching.rules -l out
```

The configuration test and offline run serve different purposes. A valid configuration can still express the wrong detection condition. The exclusive rules-file option makes this experiment's loaded rules explicit; it is not an instruction to remove a production ruleset. Preserve logs, effective configuration and the capture, inspect the actual alert output, and compare with independently labelled events. An empty alert file is ambiguous until engine startup, input processing, parser state and output configuration are verified.

## Separate packets, events and detection decisions
Choose the scoring unit before measuring performance. One TCP conversation may contain several application transactions, and one transaction may span packets or be retransmitted. Counting every mirrored packet as a distinct attack inflates the denominator. Conversely, a suppression rule may collapse several independent unauthorised operations into one alert. Correlate the chosen event identifier with capture and application evidence. Preserve duplicates as raw evidence while defining how they contribute to event-level scoring.

For a labelled binary trial, true positives are relevant events correctly detected, false negatives are relevant events missed, false positives are benign events incorrectly raised, and true negatives are benign events not raised. Precision is `TP/(TP+FP)` and recall is `TP/(TP+FN)`. State what happens when a denominator is zero rather than reporting invented perfect performance. Overall accuracy can look excellent when most activity is benign while consequential events are missed. Break results down by the paths and operations the requirement treats as critical.

Test tuning on data that did not determine the rule. If the same capture is used repeatedly to select exceptions and report performance, the estimate can reward memorisation of its particular traffic. Keep separate development and acceptance sets, preserve representative benign maintenance and failure states, and include the critical subgroup. An approved maintenance account is not a blanket reason to suppress all its future actions: its credential or session may be misused, and the requirement may limit target, time, operation and point range.

## Engineer the complete response path
A passive IDS produces observations and alerts; it does not block a command merely because an alert action appears in a rule. Inline prevention introduces forwarding, failure-mode, latency and compatibility requirements that need a separate approved design. Confirm where the engine actually runs, what path it controls and what happens on failure. A simulation of drop behaviour is not evidence that a physical OT path was blocked.

Detection latency is only part of useful response. Include collection, parsing, correlation, queue delay, analyst decision, authorised action and validation. A precise alert delivered after the process consequence has occurred may still support investigation but may fail the preventive response objective. Calculate staffing and queue behaviour under the expected and burst workloads. A tuning change that lowers alert count by hiding the highest-consequence events is not an improvement.

Capture health belongs in the acceptance evidence. Mirror oversubscription, truncated frames, dropped buffers, missing directions, unsupported encapsulations and clock errors can change conclusions. A 1 Gbit/s observation link cannot sustain 1.4 Gbit/s of copied traffic indefinitely. Increasing an alert threshold will not recover packets that never reached the parser. Record collection and processing loss separately from true detection misses, because they suggest different corrective actions.

Finally, version the detection as maintained engineering: risk/requirement reference, scope, implementation, test fixtures, expected results, known blind spots, owner, response, review triggers and rollback. Re-run relevant acceptance tests after a parser, asset map, software, route, encryption or process change. The original offline lab proves only its declared data transformations and decisions; the learner must implement and validate the selected IDS in the representative vendor/site environment before claiming operational coverage.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC DETECTION TRIAL: A passive sensor observes a mirrored primary path. Its 1 Gbit/s mirror receives a sustained 1.4 Gbit/s offered copy load during a burst. A separate labelled transaction trial contains 100 unauthorised writes and 1,000 authorised transactions: TP=60, FP=20, FN=40, TN=980. All ten writes in the critical protection-settings subgroup are among the 40 misses. The analyst takes three minutes per raised event; no batching is credited. Forty missed writes are in encrypted sessions for which the sensor has no application plaintext. A rule alerts on a SYN from H=10.20.0.10 to G=10.30.0.40 TCP/502 and its label says Write detected; it contains no industrial function match. The sensor is passive, not inline. One maintenance write appears in three packets due to a retransmission and is one labelled transaction. Tuning proposal T suppresses every event from the vendor account; acceptance data currently equals the rule-development capture. The response objective is five minutes; measured collection/detection is one minute, queue wait six minutes, analysis three minutes and approved action one minute.
worked_examples.solution:
The trial's precision is 60/80=75%, recall is 60/100=60%, and overall accuracy is 1,040/1,100≈94.55%. The high accuracy conceals zero recall in the ten-event critical subgroup. Eighty raised events require 240 analyst-minutes at the supplied rate. End-to-end response is 1+6+3+1=11 minutes, which exceeds the five-minute objective even though collection/detection is fast.

The SYN rule establishes only the supplied transport pattern; its message does not add write semantics. Passive observation also does not block the action. The encrypted cases need an explicit visibility/control design, and the mirror burst creates a separate collection-loss risk. One retransmitted transaction remains one scoring event. Proposal T can hide abuse of the vendor identity, while reusing development data fails to provide an independent acceptance trial. Preserve these as distinct findings with their own corrective tests.

guided_practice.prompt: Redesign the acceptance trial to distinguish parser visibility, critical-operation detection, benign maintenance behaviour and timely response. Calculate the original precision and critical-subgroup recall first.
guided_practice.hint: Use a labelled event denominator and examine the critical subgroup separately from aggregate accuracy.
guided_practice.solution: Original precision is 75%; critical-subgroup recall is 0/10=0%. Create held-out labelled captures and application evidence for each path/encryption mode, verify loaded rules and parser health, preserve authorised maintenance variations, and test queue/action timing. A transport-only alert is not a substitute for operation-level detection or prevention.

independent_task.brief: Implement the local offline IDS workflow where the supported engine is available, or prepare the exact rule/configuration/capture and expected-event package for a supervised session. Compare one transport rule with a justified application-aware detection and record actual evidence separately from unexecuted commands.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The event denominator and critical subgroup are explicit; duplicate packets do not inflate independent-event counts.
The report distinguishes passive detection, application visibility, collection loss and prevention.
The rule baseline, independent labelled acceptance data and complete response timing are retained.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Logging, time distribution and defensible event correlation
lessons.body:
## Define the record before selecting a collector
Logs support several different decisions: explaining a process disturbance, attributing an administrative action, recognising an incident and demonstrating a maintenance requirement. Specify the required events and fields for each decision. A useful change record identifies the asset and boot/session context, initiating principal, requested operation, affected object, result, source time, receipt time and relevant configuration version. An authentication success is not a completed configuration change; a command acceptance is not independent evidence of actuator movement. Retain these distinct stages instead of replacing them with one generic success flag.

Use stable asset and point identifiers alongside network addresses and human names. Addresses can be reused after replacement, and a common jump-host address may represent several people. Sequence numbers can detect missing or duplicate records within their defined scope, but may reset after reboot or wrap. Pair them with a boot/session identifier and document their semantics. Preserve the original record and parsing version so a later parser correction can be audited. Normalisation should add interpretation without silently deleting uncertainty or changing the source's meaning.

## Separate the time quantities
A source timestamp describes when its clock said an event occurred. A receipt timestamp describes when a collector observed the record. Neither alone is an unquestionable physical event time. Buffering, network delay, clock offset, timestamp location and application scheduling contribute different errors. Record time zone, resolution, synchronization source/status and an appropriate uncertainty or known offset. Convert presentation to UTC while retaining original evidence and conversion assumptions. If a source has no trustworthy event time, say so and use bounded receipt/order evidence rather than manufacturing precision.

For elapsed durations, a monotonic clock avoids wall-clock adjustments changing an interval unexpectedly. A wall clock is necessary for cross-system calendar correlation but can step or slew. A timeout implementation based on wall-clock subtraction may behave badly when the clock moves backward or forward. Design the operational timer and the evidence timestamp separately. NTP and PTP can support synchronization; authentication of a time message does not make every path delay symmetric or every source clock correct.

The elementary NTP four-timestamp calculation uses client send t1, server receive t2, server send t3 and client receive t4. The estimated server-minus-client offset is `theta=((t2−t1)+(t3−t4))/2`; the round-trip network delay is `delta=(t4−t1)−(t3−t2)`. Server processing time is removed from the round trip. The offset estimate depends on the assumed relationship between forward and reverse delay. Unequal paths bias the estimate; taking the reported value to many decimal places does not remove that bias. Validate the actual selected time implementation, source quality, filtering and failure behaviour.

To compare uncertain events, translate their timestamps into intervals. If A could have happened anywhere from 60 to 140 ms and B from 120 to 180 ms, those intervals overlap and the logs alone cannot establish their order. A further event bounded to 290–310 ms is later than both. Correlation should retain ambiguity where it matters to a causal claim. A recorded command after an alarm may actually precede it if their timing bounds overlap; investigate with independent sequence or physical evidence rather than choosing the preferred narrative.

## Engineer transport, persistence and semantics
Syslog has a defined message structure rather than merely an arbitrary timestamp followed by text. RFC 5424 provides a versioned header and structured-data representation. The priority value combines facility and severity as `PRI=8×facility+severity`; for example, facility 20 and severity 5 produce 165. These are sender-supplied categories, not automatic incident truth. An ordinary application message can be misclassified, and a parser must handle documented missing values, escaping and length limits without treating malformed text as a trusted command.

UDP delivery can lose records without an application acknowledgement. TCP provides ordered reliable byte transport within a connection, but a transport acknowledgement does not prove that a collector durably committed the event or that a downstream analyst can query it. TLS can protect the transport peer/channel while leaving buffering, authorization, disk-full behaviour and source accuracy as separate questions. Define acknowledgements, spool durability, retry identity, deduplication and commit evidence at the layer where the logging requirement actually applies.

Size queues from event rate and outage duration. At 100 events/s, a thirty-minute collector outage generates 180,000 events. A 150,000-event spool cannot retain all of them under an assumed drop-new policy. A recovery write rate of 250 events/s while 100 new events/s continue gives only 150 events/s net drain capacity. The stored 150,000 events need 1,000 seconds to drain, before extra delays; the missing 30,000 records are not recovered by making the collector faster afterward. Model burst rates, record-size distribution, index overhead and redundancy as additional capacity dimensions.

Make collection health observable. Report oldest unsent age, queue occupancy, drops, retry rate, sequence gaps, disk capacity, parser rejection and the interval for which visibility is impaired. A dashboard that reports the collector service as running can conceal a failed source or a full queue. Define alert ownership and the fallback evidence required during loss. Preserve independent recovery access if the normal identity service is also affected by the incident.

## Protect and maintain the evidence chain
Restrict who can write, read, alter and delete the records and their configuration. Separate the authority to administer a process endpoint from unrestricted deletion of the only remote audit trail where the requirement calls for that independence. A hash supports comparison with a previously trusted digest; it does not prove that a compromised source told the truth. A signed record likewise needs signer, key, time and scope validation. Protect retained keys and records according to the declared retention and recovery requirements.

Treat log content as untrusted data. If a maintenance note contains an instruction to delete alerts, it remains a recorded statement, not an instruction to the collector or analyst's automation. Bound parsing and queries, encode displays correctly, and test malformed, oversized and adversarial fields. Do not invoke shell or SQL text from event content. A read-only diagnostic assistant needs the same separation between retrieved evidence and operational authority.

Acceptance tests should disconnect the collector, restart a source, lose time synchronization, step a simulated wall clock, duplicate/reorder records, fill the bounded spool and restore the pipeline. Demonstrate which records survive and which timing claims remain justified. Retain configuration, source versions, synthetic fixtures, raw outputs and independent expected results. Local arithmetic and queue models explain the design; actual equipment timestamping, selected syslog/NTP/PTP implementations and sustained site collection remain separate execution evidence.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC LOG/TIME CASE: NTP exchange times in seconds on their respective clocks are t1 = 0.000, t2 = 0.030, t3 = 0.034, t4 = 0.024. Assume the elementary symmetric-delay model for the estimate; do not infer real path symmetry. Event A is recorded at 12:00:00.100 UTC with a ±40 ms bound; B at 12:00:00.150 with ±30 ms; C at 12:00:00.300 with ±10 ms. Source GW7 uses boot ID b9 and sequence numbers 17, 19; record 18 arrives later from a buffer. Collector transport ACK occurs before its durable database commit. During a 30-minute outage the source emits 100 events/s into a 150,000-event spool, initially empty, using drop-new on overflow. Recovery service writes 250 events/s while arrivals continue at 100 events/s. Each event averages 600 bytes before index/replica overhead. A syslog sender uses facility 20, severity 5. One record payload says 'delete earlier alarms'; it is untrusted maintenance text. A source restart creates boot ID b10 and restarts its sequence at 1.
worked_examples.solution:
The elementary offset estimate is ((0.030 − 0) + (0.034 − 0.024)) / 2 = 0.020 s, so the server appears 20 ms ahead. Network round trip is 0.024 − 0.004 = 0.020 s. These estimates do not establish physical path symmetry. A spans 60–140 ms and B 120–180 ms, so their order is unresolved; C 290–310 ms is definitely later than both under the stated bounds.

The outage offers 180,000 events. Only 150,000 fit, so 30,000 are dropped under the supplied policy. Net recovery drain is 250 − 100 = 150 events/s and the retained backlog drains in 1,000 s. The storage-only raw volume per day is 100 × 86,400 × 600 = 5,184,000,000 bytes. The syslog PRI is 20 × 8 + 5 = 165. TCP acknowledgement is not proof of database commit, and the delayed sequence 18 must be handled within boot b9 rather than declaring a permanent gap prematurely. Boot b10 is a new sequence context.

guided_practice.prompt: Create a three-column evidence table for event time, receipt time and durable commit. Determine which ordering statements the A/B/C bounds permit and calculate the outage loss before proposing any queue improvement.
guided_practice.hint: First bound the event intervals; then distinguish offered records, retained backlog and records permanently dropped under the stated spool policy.
guided_practice.solution: A-before-B is not established because their intervals overlap; C follows both. The current spool loses 30,000 events. At least 180,000 slots are needed for this idealised outage alone, with additional justified margin for bursts and implementation overhead. Transport receipt must not be reported as durable storage without the relevant application evidence.

independent_task.brief: Build a local timestamp/sequence and queue worksheet using the supplied case, then specify a representative collection test including clock uncertainty, durable receipt, retry identity and overflow. Use only fictional records until the actual source and collection permissions are established.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Original and normalised time fields are preserved and uncertain ordering is not presented as certain.
Queue loss and recovery duration use the net service rate with continued arrivals.
Transport, durable storage and query availability are separate observable stages with defined failure tests.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Availability architecture, failover authority and state consistency
lessons.body:
## State the service and its invariants
Availability is about a required function under defined conditions, not merely whether an address answers. A supervisory service may need current qualified measurements, a bounded alarm delay, one authorised command origin and recoverable audit history. A redundant pair can keep a web page visible while displaying stale values or admitting conflicting control actions. Write the service criteria, allowed interruption, data-loss tolerance and command-authority invariant before selecting a high-availability mechanism.

Distinguish several layers of redundancy. Link aggregation can preserve a link bundle after a member failure; a routing protocol can find another path; a firewall pair can preserve selected network state; a virtualisation cluster can restart a guest; an application pair can transfer a service role; and an independent physical train can provide process capacity. One layer's success does not establish the others. Restarting a VM is not equivalent to an application completing its recovery or the correct controller becoming authoritative. Map the dependencies from the physical function through identity, DNS, time, storage, networking and management.

Active/passive and active/active designs require explicit ownership rules. Two front ends serving read requests may be acceptable while two independent writers issuing actuator commands are not. A shared database can coordinate some operations yet remain a common failure domain. Application-level idempotency can prevent duplicate work only when its identity store and transaction semantics meet the required failure assumptions. Do not infer correct control authority from a load balancer distributing connections successfully.

## Quorum, leases and fencing solve different problems
Quorum selects which participants may make a coordinated decision under a specified failure model. A majority of three votes needs two. After a partition into groups of two and one, only the majority side can form that quorum, assuming the configured voter identities and rules behave as intended. The minority can still be running and may still have another path to equipment. Election permission alone does not prove that its earlier command authority was removed.

A lease grants authority for a bounded period under specified clock and renewal assumptions. The system must handle delayed renewals, uncertainty, pause/resume, restart and the enforcement point's view of expiry. A newly elected node cannot safely assume the old node's previously granted rights have expired merely because heartbeat traffic disappeared. A lease token that is not checked by the downstream command path is only metadata. Use the selected supported platform's actual mechanism and test its relevant failure semantics.

Fencing prevents the former owner from continuing to access the protected resource or command path. It may be implemented through a supported power, storage, access or application mechanism, but the exact target and confirmation matter. Fencing the old node's management interface may leave its process-facing interface usable. A successful fence request can precede the effective denial at the resource. The acceptance criterion should use the observable result required by the design, including what the new owner does when fencing is unavailable or its outcome is uncertain.

Witness placement also matters. A witness on the same failed power, rack, switch or management authority as one participant may not provide the assumed independent vote. More addresses do not necessarily create more failure independence. Conversely, independently located votes do not solve every Byzantine or compromised-controller problem; the relevant platform model must be understood. Record which failures the design tolerates and which result in a controlled degraded state requiring escalation.

## Reconcile recovery time with preserved authority
A fast recovery objective cannot be met by discarding the one-writer requirement. Include detection, election, removal of conflicting authority, state reconciliation, application activation and functional validation in the interruption budget. Some stages may run in parallel, but dependencies must be explicit. The earliest admissible service time is determined by the actual critical path and preconditions, not the first successful ping or leader-election message.

When the authority-removal mechanism takes longer than the allowed outage, the design has a constraint conflict. Improve the supported fencing path, change the architecture, provide a justified independent operating mode, or review the service requirement with its owner. Do not simply relabel the conflict as successful failover because connectivity returned quickly. A local controller's approved autonomous behaviour may preserve a bounded process function during supervisory loss, but its capability and limits need specific evidence.

Fail-safe behaviour is process-specific. Blocking an untrusted command is different from blindly de-energising every output. The latter can itself create an unacceptable process consequence. Define whether the local function continues, holds a qualified state for a bounded interval, transfers to an authorised local operator, sheds a load or stops under an approved protective sequence. General-purpose security automation should not invent the process response. Preserve the separation between supervisory cyber recovery and independent protective functions.

## Restore the right state, not just the role
Asynchronous replication can leave the standby behind the accepted source state. Establish which transactions were durably committed, which were replicated, which acknowledgements were returned and how incomplete operations are reconciled. A replica timestamp is meaningful only with trustworthy clock and scope. A returned acknowledgement may have promised more than the replica can recover if the design does not coordinate those guarantees.

RPO concerns the maximum acceptable loss of the relevant state; RTO concerns restoration of the required function. They are not interchangeable. A pair can meet the interruption target while losing too much configuration or history. For controls, also examine retained setpoints, sequence state, forced points, pending commands and ownership tokens. Replaying a queued command after failover can be invalid when its age, operating mode or authorisation has changed. Use explicit command identity and freshness at the enforcing application, not just transport reconnection.

Validate failback as a separate transition. The returning node may contain an old project, stale credentials, divergent database history or a still-valid queued request. It should not automatically resume command authority because its heartbeat is visible again. Reconcile its baseline and state under the supported recovery procedure, determine whether it rejoins as a replica or owner, and test the change. Preserve evidence of both the failed transition and the corrected retest.

## Prove physical and administrative independence
A surviving supervisory server cannot manufacture process capacity. If two cooling trains each provide 500 kW against an 800 kW requirement, losing one leaves a 300 kW deficit in the simple steady-state model. An otherwise perfect control failover does not close that deficit. Work with the appropriate mechanical/electrical owners on capacity, transients, protective behaviour and permitted load management; the arithmetic is only a declared simplified model.

Build a fault matrix that separately challenges node loss, one-way communications, partition, stale replica, witness loss, failed fencing, loss of shared storage, credential compromise, management-path failure and site dependencies. Record normal and alternate data paths plus the authority to change them. Two nodes on different power feeds can still share a datastore or privileged account. An out-of-band console attached to the same failed top-of-rack switch may not provide the required independent recovery path.

Acceptance evidence should combine timing traces, resource-side authority observations, configuration/state comparisons and the required application/physical outcomes. A successful nominal switchover is one case, not a complete fault qualification. Run bounded models and approved vendor simulations first, then the required representative equipment tests with defined abort conditions and responsible operators. The included synthetic exercise explains decision logic; it does not qualify a real cluster, controller, protection system or process for service.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC FAILOVER CASE: C1/C2 are supervisory command services, with witness W and a two-of-three majority rule. At t = 1 s a partition isolates C1 from C2/W, but C1 can still reach controller G. C1's last valid command lease expires at t = 8 s under the case's trusted enforcement clock. C2/W elect C2 at t = 2 s. Effective fencing of C1 at G is confirmed only at t = 5 s; a fence request was sent at t = 2 s. Requirement: at most one command authority at any time and accepted service restored within 3 s of the partition, by t = 4 s. Candidate procedure enables C2 commands immediately at t = 2 s. Assume no earlier validated revocation or lease-expiry evidence. In a separate state-loss subcase, C2's verified recoverable state ends at 12:00:00; C1 continues committing relevant events until its failure at 12:00:04, with no other verified recovery source for those later events. The state-loss limit is 2 s. This subcase does not alter the earlier partition/fencing timeline. Both service VMs use datastore DS and a shared backup administrator. Their console path and normal management path both cross switch S1. Two physical cooling trains each provide 500 kW against 800 kW steady load in a deliberately simple capacity model. A restarted C1 holds an older project and a queued write whose 5 s freshness limit has elapsed.
worked_examples.solution:
C2/W have two votes and may make the majority decision, but C1 retains a usable command path and an unexpired lease. Enabling C2 writes at t = 2 s therefore fails the one-authority invariant in the stated design. With no earlier validated revocation, the first supplied effective fence evidence is t = 5 s, earlier than lease expiry t = 8 s but later than the service deadline t = 4 s. The design must resolve that conflict rather than claiming that election alone is accepted service.

The replicated-state gap is 4 s, exceeding the 2 s loss limit. Shared DS, backup authority and S1 create separate common dependencies. In the capacity model, one surviving train provides 500 kW, leaving a 300 kW deficit. Returning C1 needs controlled reconciliation of its older project and expired queued request before any ownership decision. Each finding requires its own correction and retest; one successful ping does not close them.

guided_practice.prompt: Draw the transition preconditions from partition through election, effective fencing, state reconciliation and accepted service. Identify the conflict between exclusive command authority and the restoration deadline, then assess the separate state-loss and capacity conditions. Propose changes that preserve all applicable constraints.
guided_practice.hint: Treat majority election, removal of old authority, recoverable state and process capacity as separate evidence. Do not count a requested fence as an effective one.
guided_practice.solution: The candidate t = 2 s activation can overlap C1 authority. Waiting for the first confirmed fence at t = 5 s preserves that precondition but misses the t = 4 s deadline. Separately, the 4 s state gap exceeds 2 s. A supported faster authority-transfer design and a replication/acknowledgement strategy meeting the state-loss requirement need validation; physical capacity also needs its own approved treatment.

independent_task.brief: Create a vendor-neutral state and fault matrix for the paired service, including partition, failed fencing, stale state, failback and shared-resource loss. Prepare a representative platform test plan with resource-side observations and bounded process conditions; execute only the authorised local model or supported isolated lab.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Election, effective authority removal, state recovery and physical function have separate acceptance evidence.
The timing budget respects dependencies and does not call an unsafe early activation successful recovery.
Common physical and administrative dependencies, stale commands and failback are explicitly tested.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.
