lessons.title: Migration and cutover: authority transfer, recovery deadlines and credible rollback
lessons.body:
### Treat the transition as a designed operating state

A migration introduces states that do not exist in either the old steady-state diagram or the new one. Old and new identities may coexist, some clients may use cached destinations, data stores may have different schemas, and only part of a policy set may be active. Design these intermediate states explicitly. For each stage, identify the authoritative writer, required readers, active enforcement points, valid data source, observation path and recovery route. The transition is acceptable only if its own invariants hold, not merely because both endpoint architectures look sound.

Use a dependency graph to establish sequence. For example, establish the new trusted endpoint and required name resolution before directing clients to it; make recovery keys and the supported backup available before transforming the database; qualify the new operating role before withdrawing the old provider’s access. A sequence can contain parallel tasks only when they do not invalidate each other’s assumptions. Two teams simultaneously changing the same routing, identity or application object can create a state that neither approved plan describes.

Distinguish preparation from activation. Loading an image, allocating an address or importing a candidate policy may be preparatory; accepting process-changing requests, moving write ownership or committing a destructive schema migration is an activation boundary. Identify the last reversible point for each mechanism. Some operations are reversible by restoring configuration; others require data reconciliation, compatible software, vendor action or physical work. Never call an action reversible merely because a previous file still exists.

### Budget backward from the required recovered service

The maintenance window must include a failed attempt and its recovery. Let W be the window deadline, R the supported rollback duration, V the validation needed after rollback, and C the reserved contingency. The latest decision time for starting rollback is W - R - V - C, assuming these tasks are sequential and the durations are justified. For W=40 minutes, R=12, V=6 and C=4, the latest decision is minute 18. A forward check beginning at minute 12 and requiring eight noninterruptible minutes cannot provide its result before minute 20. If it fails, the original recovery budget is already lost.

Correct the schedule before executing that check. Options include earlier start, a shorter independently justified test, approved interruption points, a different validated recovery method or a larger approved window. Merely hoping the forward check passes is not a recovery plan. Use actual dependencies and critical-path duration rather than adding overlapping tasks twice or assuming parallelism without evidence. Record elapsed time against an agreed clock and establish who can call the rollback decision when its trigger is reached.

Recovery duration must end at accepted service, not at the installer’s completion message. Include obtaining required authority, restoring data and configuration, reestablishing trust, correcting mappings, validating the application and returning responsibility to operations. An operator or physical isolation that is only available on request is a real dependency. An outage budget that counts only file-copy time understates the required recovery path.

### Move data without losing its meaning or ownership

Define a migration consistency point. A backup captured before new writes may restore the old service but omit later records. If the rollback returns to that point, quantify the potential loss and reconcile it with the approved recovery-point objective. For a last recoverable committed event at 12:00:00 and a decision at 12:00:45, the potential uncovered interval is 45 seconds. A 30-second requirement is not met by calling the backup recent. Preserve or replay the accepted post-backup transaction stream where supported, or obtain an explicit decision about the resulting loss before proceeding.

Schema changes can make old software unable to read data written by the new version. Keep a tested compatibility matrix covering old application/old schema, new application/new schema and any proposed mixed or downgrade state. Restoring only the old binary after a noncompatible schema migration can create an unusable hybrid. A credible rollback set includes the supported data-state method and a plan for records created after migration. Changing point units or quality representation also changes semantics: do not merge histories simply because column names match.

Parallel observation is useful when it does not create parallel authority. A shadow reader can compare new and old interpretation without issuing commands. Two independently writable masters can create conflicting setpoints or duplicate operations even if both are individually healthy. Transfer authority through an approved mechanism that prevents both from acting at once and lets observers establish which source currently owns the action. Do not infer ownership solely from a route being advertised or a management service responding.

Retry behavior matters during uncertain cutover responses. A client may time out after the target accepted an operation. Reissuing it can duplicate a non-idempotent action. Use the supported transaction identity, operation-state readback or application-specific reconciliation method before retrying. A transport timeout is uncertainty about outcome, not proof that nothing happened. The migration design should specify how pending requests are drained, canceled or reconciled before the authority transition.

### Preserve security during coexistence and restoration

DNS updates do not instantly redirect every client. Resolver caching, application caches and established sessions can keep some traffic on the old endpoint. Verify both new connections and retained sessions against the required transition behavior. A six-minute cached address can outlive the planned old-service retirement even when the authoritative DNS record has changed. Record actual observed destination identity, not only the control-plane update acknowledgment.

Temporary access needs exact scope, owner, expiry and evidence of removal. A broad vendor account created for migration can survive the final configuration export unless its effective revocation is checked. Rollback must not resurrect authority known to be compromised. If the old baseline contains an exposed token, prepare a supported recovery variant that restores required function with changed trust material; test that the retired token no longer works. “Return to the old hash” is insufficient when the old trust state is unacceptable.

Use go/no-go criteria tied to observable requirements. Examples include loss of a verified alternate path, uncertain write ownership, incorrect point identity, excessive stale data, failed audit attribution or inability to finish rollback within the remaining window. Stop criteria should not be revised under schedule pressure to match a failing result. A qualified decision can change scope or risk treatment, but that is a recorded approval with consequences and new verification obligations.

After cutover, observe a defined stabilization interval under representative load and modes. Reconcile queued events, sessions, jobs, credentials and temporary routes; verify backups against the new baseline. Hand operations the exact accepted state, known restrictions, monitoring and restoration method. Migration completion is a controlled transition to sustained operation, not simply the moment the new dashboard first displays normal values.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — Synthetic cutover C24: maintenance window ends at minute 40. Supported rollback takes 12 min, post-rollback validation 6 min, contingency reserve 4 min; these stages are sequential. At minute 12 an eight-minute noninterruptible forward test is proposed. Old gateway/application A uses database schema 5; new B changes it to schema 6, which A cannot read. Backup DB0 contains committed events through 12:00:00; at decision time 12:00:45 there is no verified replay of later events. Approved recovery-point objective is 30 s. Proposal runs A and B as simultaneous command writers during comparison. A read-only shadow mode is supported. DNS now names B, but some clients retain A’s address for six minutes and existing sessions remain active. One process-changing request times out after submission; execution state is unknown. The old configuration backup includes a previously exposed support token. A temporary migration administrator account has no scheduled expiry. Required stop conditions include uncertain write ownership, wrong physical point mapping and inability to meet the recovery deadline. No live system action is authorized by this case.
worked_examples.solution:
The latest rollback decision is minute 40 - 12 - 6 - 4 = 18. The proposed forward test ends at minute 20, so starting it at minute 12 without an approved interruption or revised recovery plan loses the stated margin. Resolve the schedule before that activation step rather than assuming a pass. Restoring A’s executable alone cannot read schema 6; use the supported data-state recovery and reconcile accepted post-backup events. The uncovered interval is 45 s, exceeding the 30 s objective by 15 s.

Compare A and B with a supported read-only shadow, then transfer command ownership through an explicit verified mechanism. Do not permit two independent command writers merely to obtain a convenient comparison. DNS update acknowledgment leaves cached and established A sessions to be handled under the transition plan. Reconcile the unknown operation result before replaying a potentially non-idempotent request. Prepare recovery with rotated trust material and verify that the exposed token and temporary administrator authority are removed. A successful new dashboard is only one observation; acceptance also needs correct point identity, single authority, required monitoring and a credible recovery path.

guided_practice.prompt: Create a cutover state table and backward timeline for C24. Identify the last safe decision point, database rollback dependency, uncovered record interval, authority-transfer test and cleanup evidence.
guided_practice.hint: Budget to accepted recovered service. Separate candidate deployment from activation, and do not treat a timeout as a known failed operation.
guided_practice.solution: Latest rollback decision is minute 18; the proposed noninterruptible test would finish at 20 and needs replanning. A supported database recovery method is required for schema 5, with reconciliation of records beyond 12:00:00. Current potential loss is 45 s and fails the 30 s objective. Use read-only shadow comparison and verified single-writer transfer. Observe actual client destinations and pending request results. Rotate exposed authority, revoke temporary access and validate the full returned service.

independent_task.brief: Author a staged migration method with prerequisites, state/authority table, forward checks, timed abort points, rollback data set and stabilization criteria. Review one deliberately invalid intermediate state and explain how to correct it.

A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The schedule reserves rollback, validation and contingency before the window deadline.
Each intermediate state has one authorized writer and a known data-consistency basis.
Rollback covers compatible data, credentials, configuration and functional verification.
Temporary access, cached sessions and uncertain operations receive explicit disposition.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Acceptance and handover: preserve the design as an operationally maintained system
lessons.body:
### Accept a defined capability on a defined baseline

An acceptance decision connects the owner’s requirements to the implemented design and the evidence that it behaves as required. Start with a claim precise enough to challenge: the named maintenance role can perform approved diagnostics through the installed path, cannot execute prohibited changes, remains attributable, and has a demonstrated recovery procedure under the agreed dependency-loss conditions. A statement that the project is secure is too broad. Identify the installation, operating modes, software and configuration baseline, evidence period and remaining limitations.

Build a compact assurance structure: requirement, design argument, evidence and unresolved condition. The argument explains why the selected observations support the claim; attaching a large archive without that connection is not enough. A configuration inspection can establish a setting, a test can demonstrate behavior under particular conditions, and an operating record can demonstrate continued observation over its measured period. These forms complement one another. A passed simulator test does not become a field measurement when copied into the final report.

Maintain separate verification and validation questions. Verification asks whether the implementation meets the specified requirement; validation asks whether those requirements and the resulting system meet the intended operational need in its actual context. A remote support design can meet a narrowly written login specification and still fail the owner’s need for timely authorized recovery because the only qualified operator is unavailable. Acceptance should expose that mismatch, not conceal it behind a technically correct but incomplete specification.

### Reconcile the as-built package

The controlled baseline contains more than the newest saved files. Record effective firmware, running project and policy, hardware and I/O mappings, network paths, identities and roles, trust anchors, certificates, data schemas, alarms, time and name-service dependencies, monitoring destinations and supported recovery material. Link logical names to durable physical or platform identity. Distinguish desired, saved, deployed and observed state. A signed revision B17 stored on a workstation does not prove that a gateway still reporting active B16 enforces B17.

Use hashes to identify exact artifacts, but do not ask a hash to prove engineering correctness. Equality can show that a retrieved file matches an approved reference. It does not show that the reference has the right point map, that the device loaded it, or that it works with the installed firmware and dependencies. Preserve provenance, approval and applicability with the hash. Keep secrets out of broadly distributed diagrams and reports; record their custodian, authorized retrieval and rotation method rather than exposing reusable credentials.

Reconcile deviations before declaring an unrestricted state. Each deviation identifies the affected requirement and baseline, consequence, supporting evidence, compensating measures, responsible owner, authorized risk decision, expiry or review trigger, and closure test. Supplier acknowledgment is not necessarily owner risk acceptance. A temporary restriction can support a bounded service introduction only if the owner has authority to accept that specific residual condition and operations can maintain the credited measures. A failed required test must remain a failure even if a separate decision permits temporary operation.

### Transfer usable responsibility

Handover transfers the ability to operate and recover the design, not just ownership of files. The receiving role needs procedures, supported tools, access, skills, current dependencies, escalation routes and time to rehearse. Check that at least the required staffing arrangement can execute a recovery using individually authorized access. A document may be technically complete while all credentials and tacit knowledge remain with one departing integrator. Shared credentials should not be the shortcut used to create apparent redundancy of personnel.

Demonstrate operational tasks against representative conditions: interpret an alarm’s source and quality, review effective remote authority, restore a known baseline, validate a point mapping, rotate a supported certificate and respond to a controlled loss of monitoring. Record who performed which task and under what environment. Analytical review, emulation, vendor demonstration, supervised physical work and production observation have different fidelity and authority. The programme’s engineering identity grows from credible evidence across the lifecycle; possession of study records or certificates does not by itself authorize electrical switching, protective settings or other qualified field work.

Recovery objectives must include the actual dependency path. Suppose obtaining authorized recovery access takes 14 minutes, restoration 18, functional checks 9 and operational return 7, all sequential. The total is 48 minutes. Reporting only the 18-minute restore does not satisfy a 45-minute service recovery objective. Improvements must reduce or overlap tasks through a supported, demonstrated method, not simply remove required activities from measurement. Practice should include unavailable normal identities or infrastructure when those failures are within the recovery requirement.

### Maintain the design’s assumptions

Make the design basis operational. Record assumptions that can expire or change: firmware support, encryption trust, certificate validity, vendor response, remote access scope, available spare, data schema, time accuracy, load and remaining resilience. Assign an owner and observation method to each important assumption. A patch deferral based on a segmentation rule becomes invalid if that rule is removed during troubleshooting. The deferral remains a documented decision, but the risk supporting it must be reassessed because its credited treatment is no longer effective.

Build monitoring around required behavior and its own health. A quiet dashboard may mean no events, missing input, wrong asset association, failed collection or a disabled rule. Include heartbeat and freshness evidence, delivery errors, source counts, permission changes and service-state checks appropriate to the design. Determine how operations will distinguish loss of observation from a healthy process. Use metrics with stable definitions and denominators; reducing alarm count by excluding required sources is not demonstrated improvement.

Control change through impact analysis that follows dependencies. A gateway firmware update may alter timeout handling, supported cipher suites, point interpretation or backup compatibility. A directory group change may expand downstream engineering authority without changing any firewall. A new route can bypass a control whose own configuration is unchanged. Link the change to affected requirements and decide which prior evidence remains applicable, which requires retest and what rollback must preserve. Avoid both extremes of automatically invalidating every historical result and accepting every update solely because its product family is unchanged.

### Close and reopen the assurance argument deliberately

Define reopening triggers: an incident, failed recurring test, uncontrolled drift, changed operating mode, unsupported component, new exposure, expired exception or loss of a credited safeguard. Preserve the original acceptance decision as a historical record while recording the current limitation and corrective action. Do not rewrite the old report to imply a control always worked. Lessons learned should update requirements, design, tests and operational procedures where the cause warrants it.

Keep provider and standards claims bounded. Completion of this original course does not award the ISA certificate, certify an installation or establish a numerical achieved security level. Clause-level conformance needs the applicable licensed requirements, defined scope and appropriate assessment evidence. The technical handover can support that later work by preserving traceability and gaps. Its immediate purpose is practical: operations can identify the accepted state, recognize when its assumptions no longer hold, and restore or change it under controlled authority.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — Handover case H25: the approved package contains policy B17 with hash h17, but gateway G reports active B16. Mapping M9 and firmware 4.2 were tested together. A proposed firmware 4.3 update has no affected-behavior review. Exception E2 permits a legacy management service for 14 days, but no owner or expiry alert is assigned. A separate patch deferral credits segmentation rule S; S was removed during troubleshooting. The integrator provides a password-protected recovery archive and keeps the only recovery credential. Recovery rehearsal measurements are sequential: obtain authorized access 14 min, restore 18 min, functional checks 9 min, operational return 7 min; required service recovery time is 45 min. The final report advertises 18 min. Monitoring dashboard shows zero alerts, but one required source has had no heartbeat for six hours. A supplier signed the delivery note; the owner has not dispositioned the failed denied-write test. The project proposes calling this a certified achieved security level without a defined standards-assessment scope. These records are synthetic and do not establish a real installation’s status.
worked_examples.solution:
The current running policy is B16, so the B17 artifact hash cannot establish B17 enforcement. Reconcile the active state through the approved change and affected positive/negative tests. M9/4.2 evidence remains attached to that tested combination; assess 4.3’s changes and choose justified regression rather than assuming either complete equivalence or automatic total invalidation. E2 needs an accountable owner, expiry handling and enforceable scope. Removing S invalidates the credited risk treatment supporting the patch deferral and requires reassessment.

Handover is not usable while the receiver cannot access the recovery material independently through approved authority. The measured recovery path is 14 + 18 + 9 + 7 = 48 minutes, exceeding the 45-minute requirement by three minutes; the 18-minute figure is only one phase. Zero alerts do not demonstrate healthy monitoring when a required source is silent. The failed denied-write result remains unresolved until the authorized owner approves a defensible disposition and any required correction/retest. A delivery signature or course completion cannot establish the proposed standards-security-level claim. Preserve the evidence, conditions and explicit limits rather than granting a broader label.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a bounded acceptance decision for H25 with a current-state statement, blocking defects, possible time-limited deviations, ownership actions and required recurring checks. Calculate the actual recovery result.
guided_practice.hint: Distinguish artifact identity, effective state, functional capability, risk acceptance and credential/conformance claims.
guided_practice.solution: B17 is an approved artifact but not the reported active policy. Acceptance must resolve the denied-write failure and running-state difference. The recovery path is 48 minutes, so the 45-minute objective is not demonstrated. Assign and enforce E2’s lifecycle, reassess the patch deferral after S removal, restore monitoring-source health, and transfer usable authorized recovery access. Review 4.3’s affected dependencies before reusing M9/4.2 evidence. Any final statement must name the tested scope and unresolved limits without asserting certification or a security level unsupported by an appropriate assessment.

independent_task.brief: Prepare a handover dossier for the designed gateway service: accepted baseline, requirement/evidence index, deviations, role and dependency ownership, recovery exercise, recurring tests and change/reopening triggers.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The dossier distinguishes desired, saved, active and observed states.
Acceptance claims match evidence environment, operating conditions and exact baseline.
Residual risks have authorized decisions, owners, expiry or review triggers and closure criteria.
Receiving staff can use approved recovery access and meet measured service objectives.
Change and incident triggers lead back to affected requirements and verification.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

questions.prompt: Which project artifact should first be corrected to address K1's actual path?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — DESIGN PROJECT BASELINE (synthetic): Risk K1 is unauthorized vendor setpoint change through a cellular bypass. Requirement R1: every vendor engineering session shall traverse owner-controlled intermediary M; direct paths shall be disabled. R2: active-session revocation within 60 seconds. R3: local control shall continue during M failure; approved emergency engineering shall be available within 30 minutes without directory D. Factory baseline uses M firmware 5.1 and an independent emergency account. Site plan uses 5.2, keeps the cellular modem for commissioning, and stores emergency-account approval in an application requiring D. Factory tests show allowed session success and new-login denial after account disablement; they do not test active-session revocation or M/D loss. The installer proposes acceptance after all equipment powers on.
options: The factory login test should be repeated with another approved username only
The gateway procurement specification should require a higher encryption key length only
The architecture and access requirements must account for the cellular route and its closure or controlled mediation
explanations: Changing the tested user does not address the bypass topology.
Encryption on M does not control a separate cellular path that avoids M.
K1 is specifically a bypass path; the design must cover it before test evidence can support complete mediation.

questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC RECOVERY DESIGN: Service fails at 15:00; required RPO is 15 minutes and RTO is 105 minutes to integrated accepted operation. B1 is an independently protected, application-consistent 14:32 backup containing application 4.0/schema 4. B2 was captured at 14:55 after an unreviewed privileged startup task appeared at 14:48; B2 is immutable but its trust is unresolved. A separate file copy combines database pages at checkpoint C100 with logs beginning at C110, omitting C101–C109. Incremental chain I0→I1→I2→I3 is required by its declared restore format, but I2 is missing. Image X and its matching hash file are both writable by the production administrator. The live replica faithfully copies deletions. Backup decryption material is inside a vault that requires directory authentication; the directory recovery credential is only in that vault. Independently controlled bootstrap access has not yet been designed. Network restore takes 15 minutes, then identity takes 20. After identity, application restore takes 40 and controller restore 35; with independent qualified staff and tools those branches can run concurrently. Integrated acceptance then takes 20. A proposed cost reduction leaves one exclusive licensed workstation for both branches. B1 contains supplier-old, revoked at 14:50, and lacks service-new approved at 14:52. The controller project matches approval, but an old runtime force holds a permissive true. The host OS is clean, while BMC firmware/key trust is unknown. Application 3.0 cannot read schema 4. The backup catalogue is required by the selected restore product and is stored only on the failed primary server. Buffered genuine historian samples are available with original source timestamps; other gap values can only be estimated. Retention lock L prevents deletion for 90 days and does not permit shortening by the campaign administrator.
options: A justified provenance and chronology assessment, stated uncertainty, current-state reconciliation and targeted validation
A rule that every backup made before incident detection is automatically clean
A rule choosing the newest file solely to minimize data age

That optimizes one property while ignoring the unresolved trust of captured state.

questions.prompt: APPEND is run twice with identical desired input. Which observation disproves idempotence for the managed rule collection?
questions.exhibit:
SYNTHETIC CASE — Automation design exercise: all assets, requests and results are synthetic.

Managed service: gateways A and B carry required EPMS telemetry. Exactly one healthy gateway must remain available during the staged change. The approved plan P7 targets A identity cert-A, observed configuration revision "r17", desired policy H7, renderer T7 and a declared maintenance window. While P7 awaits execution, another approved change advances A to "r18" and the template is edited to T8. The mock HTTP API uses strong tags and returns 412 without mutation when a supplied specific If-Match tag mismatches. If-Match: * succeeds on the existence condition whenever the configuration resource exists.

Two proposed clients: APPEND adds a fresh rule object every run; SET updates one uniquely identified managed rule to its desired value. SET's current wrapper reloads A on every run, even when the semantic delta is empty. A policy list is first-match: an attempted alphabetical sort places DENY-ALL before PERMIT-EPMS although the set of rule strings is unchanged. Read-only collector C and deployer D currently share D's write credential. An imported inventory note contains a shell command; it is free text, not an approved operation.

Staging observations: an earlier health sample reports B healthy at 10:00, but live B status becomes unhealthy at 10:08 before A's 10:10 disruption. The canary used gateway model X and firmware 3; the next group includes model Y firmware 5. A supported migration permits temporary overlap only for the two named telemetry endpoints, then requires old-path removal after consumer cutover and verification.

Device A advertises candidate, validation, confirmed-commit and startup support. Device B advertises no candidate capability. A's candidate lock covers its supported local datastore, not B or plant status. A temporarily activates a new configuration under a 120-second confirmed-commit timer; required end-to-end telemetry tests have not yet passed. Its accepted running configuration has not been copied to its separate startup datastore.

Failure records: A reports its local change succeeded; B rejects its change. Separately, a POST /operations/failover request times out after transmission. In this mock API every accepted POST starts another failover sequence; the API offers an operation-status record but does not deduplicate repeated requests. The orchestrator reports the timeout as unknown, not failed. The old application A3 cannot read schema S4 created by the new application A4. A stored prior access configuration contains supplier-old, whose authority is now revoked. A dashboard displays cached desired revision H7 without a fresh device read. A proposed completion log stores full bearer tokens and only the scheduler's exit code, with no per-target outcomes.
options: The second run creates a new audit event but leaves the managed rule collection unchanged
The second run creates another rule object with the same intended policy
The second run reads the device again before finding no semantic difference
explanations: Audit activity alone does not disprove the stated configuration projection.
The collection changes again when the same operation is repeated.
A repeated observation does not itself alter the managed configuration.
